title: Docker: build, run and diagnose
prerequisites: A terminal, Docker and a local checkout
summary: Read the actual Dockerfile, observe build caching, run Makan and diagnose a failed port mapping.
text:
## The problem

“It works on my machine” usually hides a difference: runtime version, installed packages, environment variables or file paths. An image packages the application and its runtime filesystem. A container starts a process from that image with isolation and resource controls. It shares the host kernel; it is not a small virtual machine with its own kernel.

Our goal is specific: build the Makan property service once, run it locally, then deliver that same image through CI and Argo CD. PostgreSQL holds the listings and viewing requests outside the application container. Replacing an application Pod must not erase a viewing request.

## In this repository

Open `nodejs/Dockerfile`, `nodejs/.dockerignore`, `nodejs/package-lock.json` and `nodejs/compose.yaml`. The Docker build context is `nodejs/`, not the repository root. These paths are relative to the repository checkout.

```dockerfile
FROM node:24-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev && npm cache clean --force && rm -rf /usr/local/lib/node_modules/npm
COPY --chown=node:node . .
ENV NODE_ENV=production
ENV APP_VERSION=dev
USER 1000:1000
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

`FROM` chooses the runtime and base filesystem. This tag can move when its publisher updates it; a digest identifies immutable image content. CI gives our own application image a commit-based tag. Check the workflow rather than assuming a tag alone proves what is inside.

`WORKDIR` makes `/app` the working directory for following instructions and the startup command. `COPY package*.json` brings the dependency manifest and lockfile in before the application source. `npm ci` installs from that lockfile and fails if the manifest and lockfile disagree. `--omit=dev` leaves development packages out of the installed runtime dependencies.

Copying source later matters: a source edit can reuse the dependency-install cache. A lockfile edit invalidates that dependency step and the following steps. A cache is an optimization; the lockfile is the dependency record. Deleting npm from this image reduces runtime tooling, but it is not a substitute for vulnerability scanning or patching the base image.

`.dockerignore` keeps local dependencies, repository metadata and local environment files out of the build context. A secret copied into an image can survive in image layers even if a later instruction deletes it. Supply runtime secrets at runtime; do not add database URLs or administrator tokens to the Dockerfile.

`COPY --chown` controls ownership of application files. `USER` starts the service without root privileges. `EXPOSE` records the intended port; it does not publish a host port. The JSON form of `CMD` starts Node directly, so it can receive termination signals and close its HTTP server and database pool.

### Why not use a multi-stage build here?

This service runs plain JavaScript. There is no transpiled bundle or native application binary to copy out of a compiler stage. A single runtime stage is reasonable. Compare `golang/Dockerfile`: Go compiles in a builder stage, then the final image receives the executable and static web assets without the compiler. Add stages when they separate real build requirements, not simply to make every Dockerfile look the same.

### The data path

```text
Browser → published host port → Node container :3000
                                    ↓
                              PostgreSQL :5432
                                    ↓
                              named data volume
```

Inside Compose, the database hostname is the service name `database`. `localhost` inside the Node container means that Node container, not PostgreSQL and not your laptop. In Kubernetes, a Service provides the database hostname instead. The same application reads a different `DATABASE_URL` in each environment.

## Lab

Use a local checkout and Docker with Compose. This lab starts only local containers. From the repository root:

```sh
cd nodejs
cp .env.example .env
```

Edit `.env` and replace both placeholders. Use a password manager to generate a database password and a random administrator token of at least 32 characters. For this local URL, use a URL-safe database password. Do not commit `.env`.

```sh
docker compose up --build -d
docker compose ps
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/healthz
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/readyz
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3000/api/properties
```

Expect both health checks to return HTTP 200. The catalog contains six fictional homes on a new database. Open the site, filter by Maadi, open a home and submit a viewing request using sample contact details. Open the agent workspace and use your local administrator token to see the stored request. Change its status to `contacted`.

### Prove persistence rather than assuming it

```sh
docker compose restart app
```

Refresh the agent workspace and unlock it again if needed. The request and its status should still exist. The app process was replaced; the data stayed in PostgreSQL. A browser success message alone is not evidence of durable storage.

```sh
docker compose stop database
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/healthz
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/readyz
```

The existing Node process should remain alive, so liveness stays 200. Readiness should fail with 503 because the database cannot answer. A live process cannot necessarily serve business requests. Kubernetes should stop sending normal traffic to an unready Pod, rather than continually restarting it for an unavailable dependency.

```sh
docker compose start database
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3000/readyz
```

Retry readiness after the database starts. Expect recovery without rebuilding the application.

### Observe the build cache

```sh
docker build --progress=plain -t makan:lab .
docker build --progress=plain -t makan:lab .
```

The second build should reuse unchanged steps. Edit a visible sentence in `web/index.html`, rebuild, and identify the first invalidated step. Dependency installation should remain cached. Undo only your sentence edit afterward; do not discard unrelated local changes.

### Intentionally publish the wrong port

Temporarily change only the app port mapping in `compose.yaml` to `127.0.0.1:18080:9999`, keeping the valid database configuration. Recreate the app:

```sh
docker compose up -d app
curl --max-time 3 -i http://127.0.0.1:18080/healthz
docker compose logs --tail=30 app
```

Expect the HTTP request to fail even though the app can start. The process listens on 3000; publishing 9999 forwards to a port with no listener. Restore `127.0.0.1:3000:3000` and recreate the app. Change one variable at a time when diagnosing a real incident.

### Inspect runtime evidence

```sh
docker compose exec app id
docker compose exec app sh -c 'tr "\0" " " < /proc/1/cmdline'
docker compose logs --tail=30 app
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:3000/metrics
```

The user should be non-root and process 1 should run Node. Request logs contain a generated request ID and route, without contact details or tokens. Metrics use route templates rather than property slugs or request IDs, keeping the number of label combinations bounded.

### Cleanup

```sh
docker compose down
```

The named database volume is retained. Use `docker compose down -v` only when you intend to delete this lab's database, including viewing requests. A volume is persistence, not a backup. A separate backup and a tested restore address a different failure.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | First evidence | Likely next check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Image fails to build | First failing Docker build step | Lockfile consistency, registry access, build context |
| App exits at startup | App logs and required configuration | Database health, URL and administrator token length |
| Health works, catalog fails | Readiness and HTTP status | Database connectivity and initialized schema |
| Connection refused from laptop | Published mapping in Compose | Host port versus actual container listener |
| New file is absent | Rebuild output and running image | Build context, ignored files, old container |
| Request disappears after restart | Database volume and target database | Whether you recreated the volume or connected to another database |

Do not print `.env`, dump container environments into a ticket, or paste connection strings into public logs. You can verify whether configuration is present without exposing its value.

## Verify your understanding

1. Explain why `EXPOSE 3000` alone does not let your browser reach the app.
2. Show which build step reruns after a source edit and explain why the dependency step can be reused.
3. Demonstrate a viewing request surviving an app restart.
4. Demonstrate liveness succeeding while readiness fails during a database outage.
5. Explain why three application replicas need one shared database rather than three in-memory request lists.

Evidence to keep: build output, HTTP status codes, and a redacted request reference before and after restart. You have completed the lab when you can reproduce and explain these outcomes, not when you have copied all the commands.

## Arabic takeaway

الـ Image بتجهز التطبيق، والـ Container بيشغّله. الداتا مكانها قاعدة بيانات مستقلة. اتأكد من الفرق بين البورت المنشور وبورت التطبيق، وبين العملية الشغالة والخدمة الجاهزة، واثبت إن الطلب فضل موجود بعد إعادة التشغيل.

## Sources

- [Dockerfile reference](https://docs.docker.com/reference/dockerfile/)
- [Docker Compose networking](https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/networking/)

title: Git: ship a change you can undo
summary: Make a focused branch, inspect a diff, resolve a conflict and revert a change without rewriting shared history.
text:
## The problem

A deployment is easier to trust when you can answer three questions: what changed, who reviewed it, and how to undo it. Git records source history; it does not test your application or deploy Kubernetes objects by itself. Those jobs belong to the workflow and Argo CD.

A branch names a line of development. A commit records a snapshot and its parent history. A pull request is the review conversation around the proposed difference. A clean commit is useful because a reviewer and a future operator can understand one decision without reconstructing unrelated edits.

## In this repository

Read `.github/workflows/automate-build-apps.yml`, `charts/values-node.yaml` and `argocd/apps/nodejs.yaml`.

```text
Application commit → CI tests/build → image tagged with commit identity
                                    ↓
                         promotion updates Helm values
                                    ↓
                       Argo CD reconciles the cluster
```

The source commit, image reference and promotion commit are related but distinct records. A successful source build does not prove the new image has been promoted. A promotion commit does not prove the Pods have become Ready. Inspect evidence at each handoff.

A feature branch does not automatically become a production release. Check workflow event filters and the Argo CD target revision. Here, the deployment application follows `main`, and promotion changes the image tag in values.

## Lab

First inspect your working tree. Do not use reset commands to make existing work disappear.

```sh
git status --short
git log -5 --oneline
```

For practice, use a separate temporary repository so this exercise cannot accidentally promote a change to the platform:

```sh
mkdir git-delivery-lab
cd git-delivery-lab
git init -b main
git config user.name "Lab Learner"
git config user.email "learner@example.invalid"
printf 'Viewing requests are open.\n' > message.txt
git add message.txt
git commit -m "Add viewing message"
git switch -c improve-message
printf 'Request a viewing from the property page.\n' > message.txt
git diff --check
git diff
```

`git diff` shows unstaged edits. It does not show what you have already staged. Stage the exact file and inspect the proposed snapshot:

```sh
git add message.txt
git diff --cached
git commit -m "Clarify how to request a viewing"
git log --oneline --all --graph
```

### Create and resolve a real conflict

```sh
git switch main
printf 'Contact the agent to arrange a visit.\n' > message.txt
git add message.txt
git commit -m "Update agent contact wording"
git merge improve-message
```

Both branches changed the same original line. Expect a conflict, not a completed merge. Open `message.txt`, inspect the conflict markers and decide the final wording. Git cannot decide product intent for you.

```sh
printf 'Request a viewing from the property page; an agent will review it.\n' > message.txt
git add message.txt
git diff --cached
git commit -m "Merge clearer viewing instructions"
git status --short
```

The working tree should be clean. If you wanted to abandon the merge before resolving it, `git merge --abort` would return to the pre-merge state when possible. Do not continue issuing new merges while an unresolved merge is in progress.

### Undo a published-style change

Create one deliberately poor change, then reverse it with a new commit:

```sh
printf 'Viewing requests are permanently closed.\n' > message.txt
git add message.txt
git commit -m "Close viewing requests"
git revert --no-edit HEAD
git log -3 --oneline
cat message.txt
```

The last commit reverses the bad change while keeping the record. This is why `revert` is often appropriate for history others already share. A reset can move a local branch pointer; force-pushing rewritten shared history changes what colleagues see. These are different operations with different consequences.

### Connect this to GitOps rollback

Suppose the application is failing after an image promotion. Find the promotion commit and its values diff. A reviewed revert of that promotion can ask Argo CD to reconcile the previous image reference. Editing a live Deployment alone may be undone by self-heal.

Before reverting, check compatibility: an older application may not understand a newer database schema. Git can reverse a manifest edit; it cannot automatically reverse data writes or make an unsafe migration compatible.

### Cleanup

The temporary `git-delivery-lab` directory is the whole exercise. Keep it for reference or remove that directory after verifying its path. Nothing from this lab needs to be pushed.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Inspect | Next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commit contains an unrelated file | `git diff --cached --stat` | Unstage that file, then review again |
| Your edit is missing from a commit | `git diff` and `git diff --cached` | Stage the intended edit |
| Merge does not finish | `git status` | Resolve each conflict or abort the merge |
| CI passes but site is unchanged | Image tag and promotion diff | Trace promotion and Argo CD status |
| Live fix disappears | Git desired state and Argo events | Commit the intended configuration |

## Verify your understanding

Explain the difference between an unstaged edit, a staged snapshot and a commit. Show a resolved conflict with the intended final wording. Show the bad commit and its separate revert. Finally, identify the file that records the Node image tag in the real repository and explain why a source commit alone is not proof of a completed release.

## Arabic takeaway

Git سجل للتغييرات، مش نظام نشر لوحده. راجع الـ diff قبل الـ commit، وحل التعارض بناءً على المعنى. الرجوع في GitOps يبدأ من الحالة المطلوبة في الريبو، مع مراجعة توافق التطبيق وقاعدة البيانات.

## Sources

- [Git: recording changes](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Basics-Recording-Changes-to-the-Repository)
- [Git: basic branching and merging](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Basic-Branching-and-Merging)
- [Git revert](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-revert)
- [Argo CD automated sync](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/auto_sync/)

title: Cilium, Flannel and NetworkPolicy
prerequisites: kubectl, a disposable cluster with a policy-capable CNI
summary: Separate networking from ingress, test isolation and restore only the traffic your service needs.
text:
## The problem

A working network is not automatically an appropriately restricted network. A frontend needs to reach an API; that does not mean every Pod should be able to reach a database or send traffic to the internet.

Separate the questions first. A CNI connects Pods. A Service supplies a stable destination for selected backends. An ingress controller handles incoming application routing. A NetworkPolicy describes which selected Pod connections are allowed. DNS resolves names; it does not grant permission to connect.

## In this repository

Read `networking/cilium/values.yaml`, `terraform/cilium.tf`, `networking/policies/applications.yaml`, `traefik/values.yaml`, `networking/metallb/address-pool.yaml` and `golang/deploy/chart/templates/network-policy.yaml`.

```text
External browser → advertised service address → Traefik → Service → application
                                                                  ↓
                                                          database Service

Cilium: Pod connectivity and policy enforcement
MetalLB: advertise service addresses in this environment
Traefik: HTTP routing and TLS entry point
NetworkPolicy: permitted Pod traffic, not HTTP page routing
```

The learning namespace has policies for application, database, identity and monitoring traffic. The older default-namespace application policy has a broader namespace-based ingress rule. These are different scopes; do not assume every workload uses the same policy just because it is in this repository. Selectors and namespaces decide which Pods a policy actually affects.

### Why Cilium rather than Flannel?

The repository records Cilium, VXLAN tunnelling and standard NetworkPolicy. That supports a clear present-day requirement: Pod connectivity plus policy enforcement. It does not record the original selection discussion, so we cannot claim a historical benchmark or migration reason that we have not measured.

| Option | What it supplies | Tradeoff for this lab |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flannel on its own | A network fabric connecting containers across hosts | Network policy enforcement requires another component |
| Cilium | Pod networking plus standard NetworkPolicy and additional Cilium-specific policy capabilities | More features and operational concepts to understand |
| Another policy-capable CNI | An alternative implementation of networking and enforcement | Evaluate compatibility, operations, visibility and measured requirements |

Flannel is not “bad networking.” Simpler connectivity can be a valid requirement. Cilium fits the current policy exercises without adding a separate enforcement component. Do not justify it with “we need eBPF” unless you can name and demonstrate the capability you actually need. Likewise, Hubble availability must be verified from configuration; installing Cilium does not prove every observability feature is enabled.

The manifests here use standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy. Avoid switching to Cilium-specific resources until a required capability calls for them; portability and a smaller conceptual surface are useful.

### Read a policy accurately

`podSelector` selects target Pods in the policy's namespace. Once a Pod is selected for ingress isolation, permitted ingress is the union of matching allow rules from applicable policies. Egress isolation is separate. For a connection between two isolated Pods, the source egress and destination ingress must both allow it. Policies are additive; an empty allow list in one policy does not override an allow in another.

A `namespaceSelector` and `podSelector` in the same list item combine requirements. Separate list items offer alternative sources or destinations. Indentation can therefore change security meaning while still producing valid YAML.

## Lab

Use a disposable cluster with a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy. Merely accepting the resource through the Kubernetes API is not proof of enforcement. This lab creates an isolated namespace and does not modify platform policies. Confirm the current context first:

```sh
kubectl config current-context
kubectl create namespace policy-lab
kubectl -n policy-lab create deployment web --image=nginx:alpine
kubectl -n policy-lab expose deployment web --port=80
kubectl -n policy-lab run allowed --image=busybox:1.37 --labels=access=web --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl -n policy-lab run blocked --image=busybox:1.37 --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl -n policy-lab rollout status deployment/web --timeout=90s
kubectl -n policy-lab wait --for=condition=Ready pod/allowed pod/blocked --timeout=90s
kubectl -n policy-lab exec allowed -- wget -T 3 -qO- http://web
kubectl -n policy-lab exec blocked -- wget -T 3 -qO- http://web
```

Both clients should reach the nginx page initially. If not, fix baseline scheduling, image pulling, Service endpoints or DNS before testing policy. A failed baseline cannot prove isolation.

### Isolate the server

Save this as `deny-web.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: isolate-web
  namespace: policy-lab
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress: []
```

```sh
kubectl apply -f deny-web.yaml
kubectl -n policy-lab exec allowed -- wget -T 3 -qO- http://web
kubectl -n policy-lab exec blocked -- wget -T 3 -qO- http://web
```

After enforcement converges, expect both new connections to time out. The Service still exists and the server can still be Ready. The connection is denied before it reaches the HTTP application. If both succeed, inspect labels, other policies and CNI enforcement; do not declare success based on `kubectl apply`.

### Allow only the labelled client

Save as `allow-web.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-labelled-client
  namespace: policy-lab
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              access: web
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 80
```

```sh
kubectl apply -f allow-web.yaml
kubectl -n policy-lab exec allowed -- wget -T 3 -qO- http://web
kubectl -n policy-lab exec blocked -- wget -T 3 -qO- http://web
kubectl -n policy-lab get networkpolicy
```

Expect the allowed client to succeed and the blocked client to time out. The isolation policy still exists. The new allow policy adds a permitted source; it does not need to delete the isolation resource.

### Isolate client egress, then restore the necessary paths

Save as `client-egress.yaml`:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: client-egress
  namespace: policy-lab
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      access: web
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress: []
```

```sh
kubectl apply -f client-egress.yaml
kubectl -n policy-lab exec allowed -- nslookup web
```

Expect name resolution to fail: egress to DNS is now blocked too. Edit `egress` to the following and reapply:

```yaml
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              k8s-app: kube-dns
      ports:
        - protocol: UDP
          port: 53
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 53
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app: web
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 80
```

Before applying, confirm your cluster's DNS Pod labels and namespace. This example assumes CoreDNS behind the usual kube-dns Service; NodeLocal DNS or different CNI handling may require a different destination rule. The policy must match the actual packet path.

```sh
kubectl apply -f client-egress.yaml
kubectl -n policy-lab exec allowed -- nslookup web
kubectl -n policy-lab exec allowed -- wget -T 3 -qO- http://web
```

Expect resolution and the permitted HTTP request to work. You restored two separate dependencies. Opening all egress would conceal which dependency was missing.

### Cleanup

```sh
kubectl delete namespace policy-lab
```

This deletes all resources in the dedicated lab namespace. Do not substitute a namespace containing your real application.

## Troubleshooting

| Evidence | Interpretation to investigate |
| --- | --- |
| Name cannot resolve | DNS itself may be blocked or unavailable |
| Name resolves, new connection times out | Source egress, destination ingress, routes or unavailable endpoints |
| HTTP 404 or 500 | A server answered; investigate routing or the application |
| Policy exists but traffic is unchanged | Target labels, namespace, other allow policies and CNI enforcement |
| Allowed client fails after egress isolation | Both source egress and server ingress need to allow the connection |

Inspect `kubectl get pods --show-labels`, `kubectl get networkpolicy -o yaml` and `kubectl get endpointslice` in the lab namespace. If available, Cilium flow visibility can add evidence, but the lab must still be explainable without assuming an installed dashboard.

## Verify your understanding

Keep a four-row result table: baseline, ingress isolation, labelled allow, and restored egress. For each, record whether DNS works and whether each client's HTTP connection works. Explain why Flannel alone does not meet the policy enforcement requirement, and why Traefik does not replace a CNI. Finally, identify a real source-to-destination rule in this repository and explain every selector and port.

## Arabic takeaway

Cilium بيوصل الـ Pods وبيطبق السياسات؛ Traefik بيوجه طلبات الويب، وMetalLB بيعلن عنوان الخدمة. الـ NetworkPolicy لازم تتجرب باتصال مسموح واتصال ممنوع، ومينفعش ننسى DNS. اختيار Cilium مناسب لمتطلباتنا الحالية، مش دليل إن البدائل وحشة.

## Sources

- [Kubernetes NetworkPolicy](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies/)
- [Cilium policy support](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/network/kubernetes/policy/)
- [Flannel project and networking scope](https://github.com/flannel-io/flannel#networking-details)

title: AWS networking: trace the packet, prove the route
prerequisites: Linux routing and DNS; AWS CLI v2; a disposable AWS account with VPC permissions.
summary: Build a private network boundary, explain NAT versus IGW, and diagnose SG, NACL and return-path failures.

quiz.question: Which change alone makes an EC2 instance internet reachable?
choices: An IGW attached to its VPC
None: address, route and controls must all align
quiz.explanation: An IGW attachment alone supplies neither a subnet route nor a public IPv4 association.

quiz.question: Which rule set needs explicit return ephemeral-port rules?
quiz.explanation: NACLs evaluate each direction independently.

encouragement.beforeLab: Trace one connection at a time. Once the packet path makes sense, the service names become easier to remember.
encouragement.afterValidation: You have a route to follow now. Treat the next failed connection as evidence, not a reason to start over.

text:
## Learning objectives

Trace a TCP connection across subnet routes, Internet Gateway (IGW), NAT Gateway, security groups (SGs) and network ACLs (NACLs). Distinguish a missing route from a rejected packet and a failing DNS query. Produce a route/port matrix suitable for an interview whiteboard.

## Prerequisites

You already know Linux routing and Kubernetes Services. Use AWS CLI v2, jq and a dedicated sandbox account. Set a spending alert before any paid extension; an AWS Budget alerts you but is not a hard spending cap. These commands create VPC control-plane objects only, without EC2 or NAT. Read the current regional price sheet before launching the capstone. Never use this repository's production credentials.

## The problem

A private instance cannot install packages. Adding `0.0.0.0/0` to its SG does not supply a route, a NAT device, or working DNS. A public subnet means its route table points an internet default route at an IGW; it does not mean every instance has a public address. IPv4 internet access through an IGW also needs a public IPv4 association on the instance. A public NAT Gateway needs an Elastic IP and an IGW path in its public subnet; private workloads route to it and do not become internet-addressable.

An SG is stateful and attached to an ENI: allowed connection responses are tracked. A NACL is stateless, applies at the subnet boundary, and evaluates numbered rules in ascending order until a match. Allow the request destination port and the return ephemeral ports in the appropriate directions. NAT Gateways do not have SGs. Neither a NAT route nor a broad allow rule grants IAM access to S3.

For high availability, place public ingress, private app and isolated database subnets in two AZs. One NAT per AZ avoids a single egress dependency and cross-AZ routing for that design; a single NAT is a deliberate lower-cost lab compromise, not AZ-resilient egress. Gateway endpoints can keep S3/DynamoDB traffic off NAT; interface endpoints add private ENIs, DNS and per-hour/data charges.

## In this repository

Use `golang/content/labs/aws-wordpress/modules/network/` to compare a reproducible two-AZ topology to this small CLI experiment. `terraform/` at the repository root is the existing platform; do not run cloud learning commands there. Downloadable examples live under `../labs/aws-wordpress/README.md`.

## Lab

Start a fresh shell. Choose a permitted region explicitly and record the caller account before creating anything:

```bash
export AWS_PROFILE=cloud-lab
export AWS_REGION=eu-west-1
aws sts get-caller-identity --query '{Account:Account,Arn:Arn}'
VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.42.0.0/16 --query Vpc.VpcId --output text)
aws ec2 create-tags --resources "$VPC_ID" --tags Key=Purpose,Value=cloud-learning
aws ec2 modify-vpc-attribute --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" --enable-dns-support '{"Value":true}'
AZ=$(aws ec2 describe-availability-zones --filters Name=state,Values=available --query 'AvailabilityZones[0].ZoneName' --output text)
SUBNET_ID=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" --cidr-block 10.42.10.0/24 --availability-zone "$AZ" --query Subnet.SubnetId --output text)
RT_ID=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" --query RouteTable.RouteTableId --output text)
ASSOC_ID=$(aws ec2 associate-route-table --subnet-id "$SUBNET_ID" --route-table-id "$RT_ID" --query AssociationId --output text)
IGW_ID=$(aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --query InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId --output text)
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" --internet-gateway-id "$IGW_ID"
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id "$RT_ID" --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id "$IGW_ID"
aws ec2 describe-route-tables --route-table-ids "$RT_ID" --query 'RouteTables[0].Routes'
```

Draw the route before calling the subnet public. Now deliberately remove only this sandbox default route:

```bash
aws ec2 delete-route --route-table-id "$RT_ID" --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0
aws ec2 describe-route-tables --route-table-ids "$RT_ID" --query 'RouteTables[0].Routes'
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id "$RT_ID" --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id "$IGW_ID"
aws ec2 describe-network-acls --filters Name=vpc-id,Values="$VPC_ID" --query 'NetworkAcls[].Entries'
```

A new VPC's default NACL allows traffic; a custom NACL starts with deny rules. Write a proposed custom NACL matrix for HTTPS client egress: outbound destination 443, inbound client ephemeral ports, plus app/database flows separately. Do not attach an untested custom NACL to a live subnet. In the capstone, enter the app through SSM, run `getent hosts wordpress.org`, `curl -I https://wordpress.org`, `ip route`, and compare the instance route with the VPC route table. The OS default gateway alone cannot reveal the VPC's NAT target.

## Validation

The explicit table must contain the VPC-local route and the IGW default route after recovery. The subnet has no auto public IPv4 mapping and no instance: claiming successful internet connectivity here would be false. Save the caller account, route tables and a directional SG/NACL matrix, redacting account identifiers before sharing. After the capstone, test one app instance in each AZ and document whether an egress failure affects one or both.

## Troubleshooting

| Evidence | Next test | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DNS lookup fails | VPC DNS attributes and resolver | Do not diagnose NAT before name resolution |
| TCP timeout to a numeric IP | Actual subnet association, route target, SG egress, NACL return range | A route in a different table is irrelevant |
| Private app works in only one AZ | Compare private tables and NAT AZs | Often an asymmetric configuration |
| S3 returns AccessDenied | Caller identity, endpoint policy, bucket/IAM policy | HTTP response proves transport, not authorization |

Use VPC Flow Logs and Reachability Analyzer for controlled paid extensions. Flow logs show accept/reject metadata, not application payload or every DNS interaction. A network path analysis does not prove an HTTP process is listening.

## Cleanup

Use the IDs from this shell only, in dependency order:

```bash
aws ec2 disassociate-route-table --association-id "$ASSOC_ID"
aws ec2 delete-subnet --subnet-id "$SUBNET_ID"
aws ec2 delete-route-table --route-table-id "$RT_ID"
aws ec2 detach-internet-gateway --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" --internet-gateway-id "$IGW_ID"
aws ec2 delete-internet-gateway --internet-gateway-id "$IGW_ID"
aws ec2 delete-vpc --vpc-id "$VPC_ID"
```

If interrupted, find the tagged VPC, inspect its dependencies, and recover IDs before deleting. This lab never allocates Elastic IPs or NAT Gateways; if you added them yourself, release/delete them explicitly after checking ownership.

## Interview preparation

**A private EC2 instance has an allow-all outbound SG but HTTPS times out. What next?** Resolve DNS, identify its ENI and actual subnet route-table association, check the default route's NAT state, the NAT's public-subnet IGW route, then both NACL directions. Correlate flow logs. Do not fix an unproven routing failure by opening inbound SSH.

**Why SG references instead of subnet CIDRs between ALB and app?** They express identity of the participating ENIs and survive IP changes. They are not transitive and do not create routes. Use CIDRs where the traffic source cannot be represented by the intended SG relationship.

**Would you deploy one NAT or two?** Quantify required AZ availability, hourly/data/cross-AZ costs and endpoint alternatives. Explain the single-AZ egress failure domain rather than answering with a universal rule.

## Verify your understanding

Without notes, draw the outbound request and return packet, including ephemeral ports. Explain why moving the same ENI rules to another subnet can change reachability. Completion evidence: route diff, restored route, cleanup confirmation and a three-minute incident explanation.

## Arabic takeaway

ابدأ بتتبّع الباكت والـ route table المرتبطة فعلًا بالـ subnet. الـ SG stateful والـ NACL stateless؛ فتح البورت لوحده مش بيعمل route. الـ NAT للخروج من الشبكة الخاصة، والـ IGW جزء من مسار الإنترنت للشبكة العامة.

## Sources

- [VPC route tables](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/VPC_Route_Tables.html)
- [Security groups and NACL comparison](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/infrastructure-security.html)
- [NAT troubleshooting](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/nat-gateway-troubleshooting.html)

title: AWS identity: roles, STS and secret boundaries
prerequisites: AWS 01; sandbox IAM role-management permissions; AWS CLI v2 and jq.
summary: Separate trust from permissions, evaluate least privilege, and retrieve secrets through a workload role rather than embedded credentials.

quiz.question: AssumeRole succeeds but GetSecretValue fails. Which boundary passed?
quiz.explanation: Obtaining a session does not grant every service action.

quiz.question: Does Terraform sensitive=true remove a password from state?
quiz.explanation: Sensitive controls presentation; state and plan access still need protection.

encouragement.beforeLab: Start with one identity, one action and one resource. Clear boundaries beat a policy full of guesses.
encouragement.afterValidation: A denied request can be a successful security test. Explain which boundary held before changing it.

text:
## Learning objectives

Explain who may assume a role versus what that role may do. Diagnose identity-policy, resource-policy and organization-boundary denies. Retrieve a secret without printing its payload. Map Kubernetes workload identity concepts to EC2 instance profiles and STS sessions.

## Prerequisites

Complete AWS 01. Work in an account where an administrator has permitted a lab role prefix. You need IAM create/delete/simulate permissions only within that sandbox. Do not add AdministratorAccess as a troubleshooting shortcut. The local policy lab creates no secrets or compute. Secret inspection later uses only the capstone's generated secret.

## The problem

A role is not a long-lived access key. Its trust policy permits a principal to request an STS session; its permissions policy authorizes actions after assumption. An EC2 instance profile delivers role credentials through instance metadata. IMDSv2 reduces metadata abuse but does not compensate for a role allowed to read every secret. Workloads should ask the SDK credential chain for credentials and handle rotation rather than copy credentials into `.env`.

Identity policies, resource policies, session policies, permissions boundaries and service control policies can all constrain effective access. Explicit deny wins. Same-account and cross-account evaluation differ; cross-account access generally needs both sides to allow. KMS adds another authorization boundary for customer-managed keys. A Secrets Manager allow does not automatically supply `kms:Decrypt` where that key requires it.

## In this repository

The capstone's `main.tf` grants `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` for one RDS-managed secret, uses the EC2 service principal in its trust policy, and enables IMDSv2 in the launch template. Existing app secrets under `sealed-secrets/` are unrelated. Never copy those into the cloud labs.

## Lab

Confirm identity, then write a trust document and a scoped permissions document. Substitute the account returned by STS, not an account copied from a tutorial:

```bash
export AWS_PROFILE=cloud-lab AWS_REGION=eu-west-1
ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
cat > /tmp/cloud-lab-trust.json <<'JSON'
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"ec2.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}
JSON
cat > /tmp/cloud-lab-secret-policy.json <<JSON
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":"secretsmanager:GetSecretValue","Resource":"arn:aws:secretsmanager:${AWS_REGION}:${ACCOUNT_ID}:secret:cloud-lab-*"}]}
JSON
ROLE_ARN=$(aws iam create-role --role-name cloud-learning-instance --assume-role-policy-document file:///tmp/cloud-lab-trust.json --query Role.Arn --output text)
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name cloud-learning-instance --policy-name OneSecretPrefix --policy-document file:///tmp/cloud-lab-secret-policy.json
aws iam simulate-principal-policy --policy-source-arn "$ROLE_ARN" --action-names secretsmanager:GetSecretValue secretsmanager:DeleteSecret --resource-arns "arn:aws:secretsmanager:${AWS_REGION}:${ACCOUNT_ID}:secret:cloud-lab-example" --query 'EvaluationResults[].{Action:EvalActionName,Decision:EvalDecision}'
```

Expect GetSecretValue allowed and DeleteSecret implicitly denied in this identity-policy simulation. Repeat against a secret ARN outside the prefix: GetSecretValue should be denied. The IAM simulator is useful evidence about the supplied policy, not proof of end-to-end live access or all SCP/resource-policy effects.

Try explaining why `aws sts assume-role --role-arn "$ROLE_ARN" ...` from your human CLI is denied: the trust principal here is EC2, not your human identity. Do not change it to `Principal: "*"` to make a test pass. For a real STS experiment, have the sandbox administrator supply a separate role that trusts your exact lab principal and grants read-only access; call `aws sts assume-role --role-arn "$READONLY_ROLE_ARN" --role-session-name interview-lab --query 'AssumedRoleUser.Arn'`. This proves assumption without exposing temporary keys.

After the capstone is deployed by the learner, enter an app instance using SSM and run:

```bash
aws sts get-caller-identity --query Arn --output text
aws secretsmanager describe-secret --secret-id "$LAB_SECRET_ARN" --query '{Rotation:RotationEnabled,LastChanged:LastChangedDate}'
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id "$LAB_SECRET_ARN" --query VersionId --output text
```

The instance role intentionally allows GetSecretValue only; DescribeSecret may be denied. Record that as least-privilege evidence, not a broken app. Never request `SecretString` in shared terminal output. The bootstrap consumes it in memory to create a local configuration file.

## Validation

Keep the three simulator decisions and role ARN with the account redacted. Verify the policy does not allow deletion or unrelated secrets. On EC2, verify an assumed-role identity instead of an IAM user's access-key identity. Confirm the secret value is absent from user data, Terraform outputs and captured logs. The RDS-managed password remains service-managed; local app configuration must be refreshed if it rotates.

## Troubleshooting

| Failure | Investigate | Recovery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AssumeRole AccessDenied | Caller identity, trust principal/conditions, caller permission | Fix the narrow trust or permission, not both blindly |
| GetSecretValue AccessDenied | Exact resource ARN and suffix, boundary/SCP, KMS key | Grant only missing scope after evidence |
| SDK has no credentials | Instance profile attachment, IMDS settings, credential-chain overrides | Remove stale environment keys; restore profile |
| Secret works until rotation | Cached credential lifetime and application reload | Refresh/reload configuration; plan overlap |

## Cleanup

```bash
aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name cloud-learning-instance --policy-name OneSecretPrefix
aws iam delete-role --role-name cloud-learning-instance
rm -f /tmp/cloud-lab-trust.json /tmp/cloud-lab-secret-policy.json
```

If you created an instance profile, remove its role and delete the profile before deleting the role. Do not delete the capstone role from this lab's commands; Terraform owns that separate role.

## Interview preparation

**Trust policy versus permission policy?** Trust determines who can obtain a session; permissions determine what the session can do. A successful assumption followed by S3 AccessDenied proves the first boundary passed, not the second.

**How do you reduce CI credential risk?** Use federation with short sessions, repository/environment-scoped trust, least-privilege roles, protected approvals and isolated state. Avoid access-key rotation chores by not issuing static CI keys.

**Is a masked Terraform output enough for secrets?** No. Sensitive values can still be stored in state and plans. Use workload retrieval, encrypted restricted state, and secret-safe logs. Marking a value sensitive changes display, not its persistence.

## Verify your understanding

Present an allow/deny matrix for two actions and two resources. Explain why a successful IAM simulation can still fail in a live organization. Demonstrate cleanup and identify which policy grants each permission used by the capstone.

## Arabic takeaway

الـ trust policy بتحدد مين يلبس الـ role، والـ permissions بتحدد يعمل إيه بعد كده. استخدم credentials مؤقتة من STS وخلّي التطبيق يقرأ secret محدد بهويته، بدل ما تحط مفاتيح ثابتة في الكود أو اللوجات.

## Sources

- [IAM policy evaluation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html)
- [Temporary role credentials](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_temp_use-resources.html)
- [Secrets Manager permissions](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/secretsmanager/latest/userguide/auth-and-access.html)

title: AWS compute: ALB health, launch templates and recovery
prerequisites: AWS 01–02; Terraform CLI; optional learner-deployed capstone for runtime drills.
summary: Operate EC2 behind an ALB, distinguish probe success from readiness, and diagnose Auto Scaling replacement loops.

quiz.question: A DB outage makes every deep probe fail. Should EC2 replacement be the primary repair?
choices: No, isolate the shared dependency failure
quiz.explanation: Replacing healthy processes does not restore a shared database and can amplify disruption.

quiz.question: Does a new launch-template version update all existing instances automatically?
choices: No; use a controlled replacement/refresh strategy
quiz.explanation: Templates define future launches. Existing instances need an explicit rollout.

encouragement.beforeLab: Make the smallest failure you can observe. A short, clear recovery timeline teaches more than a large uncontrolled outage.

text:
## Learning objectives

Connect launch-template versions to ASG replacements, trace ALB-to-target reachability and prove recovery of a two-AZ service. Choose health signals and CloudWatch alerts that reveal user impact instead of merely reporting a running process.

## Prerequisites

Read AWS 01 and 02 and inspect the capstone files before paying for compute. Static review is available without a cloud account. Runtime commands below require a learner-deployed disposable capstone from AWS 07 and its Terraform outputs. Use a short test window and preserve evidence before destroying the lab.

## The problem

Two EC2 instances are not automatically a highly available application. They need independent AZ placement, healthy target registration, shared durable state, valid routing and enough spare capacity. Launch templates describe future instances; updating a template does not silently rebuild every existing instance. Use a controlled instance refresh and observe the rollout rather than manually patching pets.

ALB operates at HTTP layer 7: it evaluates listeners, rules and target groups. Health checks use their configured port/path and accepted status range. A redirecting login page can accidentally look healthy, while a DB-dependent probe can trigger replacement storms during a transient database outage. This capstone's `/healthz.php` checks PHP and the shared filesystem; `/readyz.php` additionally queries MySQL. ALB uses the shallow health endpoint, and you monitor deep readiness separately. ASG ELB health checks replace unhealthy targets after a grace period; bootstrapping slower than that grace produces an endless replacement loop.

## In this repository

Read `labs/aws-wordpress/main.tf` for the HTTPS listener, target SG relationship, target-group health check, launch template, two-instance ASG and CloudWatch unhealthy-host alarm. The bootstrap in `user-data.sh.tftpl` installs the web stack, mounts EFS, verifies a WordPress archive hash and retrieves the database secret at runtime. It is a transparent learning bootstrap; production should bake a patched, tested AMI and rehearse upgrades.

## Lab

Start with a no-credentials review:

```bash
cd golang/content/labs/aws-wordpress
terraform init -backend=false
terraform validate
rg 'health_check|health_check_grace_period|metadata_options|instance_refresh' main.tf
```

For the optional deployed drill, set IDs from your own outputs:

```bash
TG_ARN=$(terraform output -raw target_group_arn)
ASG_NAME=$(terraform output -raw asg_name)
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn "$TG_ARN" --query 'TargetHealthDescriptions[].{Instance:Target.Id,State:TargetHealth.State,Reason:TargetHealth.Reason}'
aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups --auto-scaling-group-names "$ASG_NAME" --query 'AutoScalingGroups[0].Instances[].{ID:InstanceId,AZ:AvailabilityZone,Health:HealthStatus}'
INSTANCE_ID=$(aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups --auto-scaling-group-names "$ASG_NAME" --query 'AutoScalingGroups[0].Instances[0].InstanceId' --output text)
aws ssm start-session --target "$INSTANCE_ID"
```

Inside that sandbox instance inspect `sudo cloud-init status --long`, `sudo journalctl -u httpd --no-pager -n 40`, `findmnt /var/www/html`, `curl -i http://localhost/healthz.php` and `curl -i http://localhost/readyz.php`. A boot error must be diagnosed before manipulating ALB matchers. Exit the session when done.

Controlled failure: in the lab only, stop Apache on one target with `sudo systemctl stop httpd`. Time the sequence: failed target checks, removal from serving traffic, ASG health change, replacement and recovery. Send HTTPS requests through the lab hostname during the event. Do not use SSH from the public internet. If you want a shorter drill without waiting for replacement, restart Apache immediately; record which recovery mechanism you actually exercised.

For a release exercise, change a non-secret bootstrap marker, plan, and inspect the new launch-template version plus ASG instance-refresh settings. Apply only after reviewing the separate AWS 07 cost gate. Use `aws autoscaling describe-instance-refreshes --auto-scaling-group-name "$ASG_NAME"` to follow progress. Capacity headroom and warmup control availability; a plan alone cannot prove zero downtime.

## Validation

Expect two healthy targets in distinct AZs after stabilization and HTTPS 200 for both health endpoints. Record outage duration, healthy-host count and replacement instance ID. Explain why an ALB health success is weaker than a successful WordPress database transaction. The included CloudWatch alarm enters ALARM if any target is unhealthy; it has no notification action until you connect an approved destination.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Evidence | Correction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Target timeout | App listener, ALB SG→app SG, NACL | Restore actual flow; don't widen all ports |
| Target response-code mismatch | Curl exact path and Host behavior | Fix endpoint/matcher contract |
| Repeated EC2 replacement | Cloud-init log, ASG activity, grace period | Fix bootstrap; choose realistic warmup |
| Healthy ALB, WordPress DB error | Deep probe, DB SG and credentials | Repair dependency, not listener |
| No SSM session | Agent status, profile, HTTPS egress/endpoints | Restore management path without public SSH |

CloudWatch metrics and alarms are not log shipping. EC2 application logs remain local unless an agent or another shipping path is configured; preserve them before instance replacement. CPU-based scaling is a starting signal, not a substitute for testing request latency and database capacity.

## Cleanup

Stop load generators and sessions. Revert the bootstrap marker if it was only an experiment. Use AWS 07's Terraform destroy procedure for the full stack; do not terminate individual resources behind Terraform and then abandon state. Confirm the ASG is gone so it cannot recreate instances.

## Interview preparation

**ALB 502 versus 503?** A 502 often involves an invalid/closed upstream response; a 503 can mean no usable registered targets. Inspect ALB access logs, target health reason codes, application logs and timing before concluding. Neither code uniquely identifies an SG issue.

**How do you roll out EC2 changes?** Publish an immutable image/template version, plan a bounded refresh with healthy capacity, monitor user-facing and dependency signals, and abort or roll forward to a known-good version. Database migrations need a compatible separate strategy.

**Why not replace every instance when the DB fails?** Replacement cannot repair a shared database outage and can amplify load. Separate process health from deep dependency monitoring and bound recovery actions.

## Verify your understanding

Explain a failed request from TLS listener to target process. Present a timeline of the controlled failure with evidence, then explain the difference between target removal, instance replacement and actual application recovery.

## Arabic takeaway

الـ ASG بيحافظ على العدد، والـ ALB بيختار targets سليمة، لكن التطبيق محتاج state مشتركة وhealth checks مناسبة. تحديث launch template لوحده مش معناه إن كل السيرفرات اتحدثت؛ راقب instance refresh وأثره على المستخدم.

## Sources

- [ALB target health checks](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/target-group-health-checks.html)
- [ASG instance refresh](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/asg-instance-refresh.html)
- [CloudWatch alarms](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/AlarmThatSendsEmail.html)

title: AWS data: RDS, S3, recovery and cost tradeoffs
prerequisites: AWS 01–03; AWS CLI; optional capstone RDS and a learner-owned S3 test bucket.
summary: Distinguish availability from recovery, test versioned object restoration, and design measurable RPO/RTO for WordPress.

quiz.question: What protects against an application deleting valid rows?
choices: Tested backups/PITR with a cutover runbook
quiz.explanation: Availability replicas do not preserve independent historical application state.

quiz.question: Does deleting current objects empty a versioned bucket completely?
choices: No, retained versions and markers remain
quiz.explanation: Old versions and delete markers must also be considered.

encouragement.beforeLab: Recovery is a skill you can practise. Begin with one harmless object and prove that the original bytes come back.
encouragement.afterValidation: A tested restore is worth keeping in your notes. Be clear about what you recovered and what still needs a rehearsal.

text:
## Learning objectives

Explain RDS Multi-AZ failover, backups and point-in-time restore (PITR) as separate mechanisms. Recover a versioned S3 object, define a WordPress consistency boundary across database and uploads, and defend an architecture's recurring cost.

## Prerequisites

Use a disposable account and AWS CLI v2. S3 storage and API calls may incur small charges; RDS, snapshots, replication and failover drills incur additional charges. No commands in this lesson should target an organizational backup bucket. Use a unique lab bucket and the same explicit region as earlier modules.

## The problem

Multi-AZ reduces a failure domain; it does not undo a malicious DELETE or a broken schema migration. A standard RDS Multi-AZ DB instance has a synchronous standby for availability, not a read-scaling endpoint. Read replicas serve a different purpose and can lag. A snapshot is a point in time; PITR uses retained backups/logs to restore a new DB instance within a supported window. Restoring creates a new endpoint and demands application cutover, credential checks and validation.

WordPress has two state stores: MySQL for posts/settings and the uploads filesystem. Restoring one without the other may leave broken media references. EFS sharing solves cross-instance visibility, not backup consistency. Choose an RPO (acceptable data loss interval) and RTO (acceptable service restoration time), coordinate a maintenance/write freeze where necessary, and measure end-to-end restore rather than only resource creation.

S3 versioning retains old versions and delete markers; it is not immutable backup by itself. An authorized attacker who can delete versions can still destroy data. Object Lock and separate-account copies address stronger threats but introduce retention and operational constraints. Encryption does not replace access control or deletion protection.

## In this repository

The AWS capstone uses RDS Multi-AZ with seven-day automated backup retention and encrypted EFS. Its short-lived lab destroy skips a final snapshot deliberately; a real deployment must change that lifecycle decision. `terraform/` and the live PostgreSQL database are outside this exercise. Do not restore or snapshot the production learning application.

## Lab

Create a versioned bucket containing only a harmless local text file. Use the bucket's versioned API to prove recovery rather than assume it:

```bash
export AWS_PROFILE=cloud-lab AWS_REGION=eu-west-1
BUCKET="cloud-learning-$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)-$(date +%s)"
aws s3api create-bucket --bucket "$BUCKET" --region "$AWS_REGION" --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint="$AWS_REGION"
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket "$BUCKET" --public-access-block-configuration BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket "$BUCKET" --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
printf 'revision one\n' > /tmp/cloud-learning-object.txt
VERSION_ONE=$(aws s3api put-object --bucket "$BUCKET" --key evidence.txt --body /tmp/cloud-learning-object.txt --query VersionId --output text)
printf 'bad revision\n' > /tmp/cloud-learning-object.txt
aws s3api put-object --bucket "$BUCKET" --key evidence.txt --body /tmp/cloud-learning-object.txt --query VersionId
aws s3api get-object --bucket "$BUCKET" --key evidence.txt --version-id "$VERSION_ONE" /tmp/cloud-learning-restored.txt
cmp /tmp/cloud-learning-restored.txt <(printf 'revision one\n')
```

The `LocationConstraint` example excludes us-east-1, which uses a different create-bucket request. Use the documented region-specific form rather than rerun blindly. For future buckets, explicitly configure default encryption and a TLS-only bucket policy as additional review tasks.

For a deployed capstone, inspect recovery capability without retrieving any password:

```bash
DB_ID=$(terraform -chdir=golang/content/labs/aws-wordpress output -raw db_identifier)
aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier "$DB_ID" --query 'DBInstances[0].{MultiAZ:MultiAZ,Public:PubliclyAccessible,Encrypted:StorageEncrypted,Retention:BackupRetentionPeriod,LatestRestorable:LatestRestorableTime}'
aws rds describe-db-snapshots --db-instance-identifier "$DB_ID" --query 'DBSnapshots[].{ID:DBSnapshotIdentifier,Status:Status,Time:SnapshotCreateTime}'
```

Design a separately budgeted restore rehearsal: choose a time before a lab-only bad write; use `restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time` with a new target identifier, private subnet group and correct SGs. Wait for readiness, configure secret access, compare expected posts and media checksums, then rehearse DNS/config cutover. Do not execute a restore until you have budgeted the additional DB and chosen a target ID; include its deletion in the cleanup inventory. A successful API call without restored application data is not a passed DR test.

## Validation

`cmp` must exit zero for the restored object. Inventory all object versions and document how a delete marker differs from removing a version. Record RDS's latest-restorable time and compare it to the stated RPO, allowing for backup/log delay. For DR interview evidence, keep a timed runbook: detect, decide, restore DB and files, validate, cut over, observe. Static review alone cannot substantiate a measured RTO.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Check | Consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S3 object 'disappeared' | Versions and delete markers | Restore a retained version instead of recreating blindly |
| RDS failover causes app errors | DNS caching, connection retries, transaction retry semantics | Existing connections must reconnect |
| Restore is complete, app empty | Database name, restored timestamp, new endpoint | Infrastructure status is not data validation |
| Unexpected bill after destroy | Snapshots, EIPs, NAT, endpoints, old object versions | Inventory residual resources, not just EC2 |

Cost review: list ALB hours/LCUs, two NAT hours/data, two EC2 instances/EBS, Multi-AZ RDS/storage/backups, EFS storage, public IPv4, CloudWatch and transfer. Prices, quotas and region availability change. Compare two-AZ requirements to a temporary single-AZ learning alternative explicitly; never market the HA capstone as free-tier.

## Cleanup

Delete **every version and delete marker** in this dedicated bucket before deleting it. `aws s3 rm --recursive` alone does not remove old versions. This sample uses one delete request, sufficient for this two-version lab; production inventories need pagination/batching.

```bash
aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket "$BUCKET" --output json | jq '{Objects:([.Versions[]?,.DeleteMarkers[]?] | map({Key,VersionId})),Quiet:true}' > /tmp/cloud-learning-delete.json
aws s3api delete-objects --bucket "$BUCKET" --delete file:///tmp/cloud-learning-delete.json
aws s3api delete-bucket --bucket "$BUCKET"
rm -f /tmp/cloud-learning-object.txt /tmp/cloud-learning-restored.txt /tmp/cloud-learning-delete.json
```

Delete any extra restored DB and manual snapshot only after confirming they are lab-owned and no recovery evidence depends on them. Use the capstone destroy for Terraform-owned resources.

## Interview preparation

**Multi-AZ versus backup?** Multi-AZ addresses infrastructure availability. Backups and PITR address recovery from historical data loss. A logical corruption can reach the standby immediately; retain and test recoverable history.

**What does a credible RTO include?** Decision and provisioning time, data validation, application/secret reconfiguration, DNS cutover and user-facing checks. Reporting only snapshot restore time understates recovery.

**How would you cut costs safely?** Measure usage, rightsize and schedule disposable labs, investigate NAT/endpoints and transfer, choose retention intentionally, then consider commitment discounts for stable usage. Keep the availability/SLO tradeoff visible.

## Verify your understanding

text:
## Learning objectives

Separate Terraform's dependency graph from cloud readiness. Design module interfaces, protect remote state and locks, interpret detailed plan exit codes and choose between reconciling configuration, import and intentional drift adoption.

## Prerequisites

Use Terraform 1.10+ for S3 native lockfiles and a sandbox role. Backend initialization downloads providers and can contact a backend; it is not an offline operation. You can run fmt and schema validation without provisioning resources. The backend bucket must be bootstrapped outside the workload state so destroying a workload cannot destroy its own state storage.

## The problem

State maps Terraform addresses to remote resources and can contain sensitive attributes. A private Git repository is not a state backend. Encryption at rest, restricted IAM, versioning, locking and recovery procedures all matter. Workspaces separate state namespaces but do not alone separate AWS accounts or IAM roles. Provider credentials and backend credentials are resolved separately.

The capstone extracts its network into a module with explicit VPC/subnet outputs. It leaves application resources visible in the root for review. A module should encapsulate a cohesive lifecycle, not wrap every resource in a one-line abstraction. Changing a subnet CIDR, resource address or immutable property can replace resources; inspect the plan's replacement paths. Use `moved` blocks to refactor addresses with continuity and import blocks for intentionally adopted existing resources.

## In this repository

Only work in `golang/content/labs/aws-wordpress/`. Read `modules/network/main.tf` and its variables/outputs. Root `terraform/` is a different infrastructure lifecycle and must not receive these providers, backend settings or cloud state. `backend.s3.tf.example` is deliberately inactive until copied by the learner.

## Lab

Start with the local state backend and schema checks:

```bash
cd golang/content/labs/aws-wordpress
terraform fmt -check -recursive
terraform init -backend=false
terraform validate
terraform providers
```

For remote state, have your sandbox administrator create a dedicated private, encrypted, versioned S3 bucket and grant scoped state-object access plus Get/Put/Delete for the `.tflock` object. Do not grant DeleteObject on historical state versions to ordinary apply roles. Copy the backend example and initialize with non-secret parameters:

```bash
cp backend.s3.tf.example backend.tf
terraform init -migrate-state \
  -backend-config="bucket=$LAB_STATE_BUCKET" \
  -backend-config="key=cloud-learning/wordpress/terraform.tfstate" \
  -backend-config="region=$AWS_REGION"
```

The example enables `use_lockfile = true`. DynamoDB-based S3 locking is deprecated in current HashiCorp guidance. Store credentials in the AWS credential chain, never backend arguments or committed files. If migrating an existing state, back it up in a private location, verify lineage/serial and inventory resources after migration; do not create a second state independently for the same live resources.

After the optional AWS 07 deploy, change only the `Purpose` tag of your lab VPC through the console. Detect the controlled drift without accepting it:

```bash
set +e
terraform plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode -out=drift.tfplan
PLAN_EXIT=$?
set -e
case "$PLAN_EXIT" in
  0) echo 'No drift' ;;
  2) echo 'Drift found: inspect the plan' ;;
  *) echo 'Plan failed; this is not a clean bill of health'; exit "$PLAN_EXIT" ;;
esac
terraform show drift.tfplan
terraform plan -out=reconcile.tfplan
```

A refresh-only plan proposes updating state to observed reality; applying it does not restore declared configuration. A normal plan shows the actions needed to reconcile the tag. Restore via a reviewed normal apply in the sandbox or intentionally update the code; document the choice. Plan files can contain secrets, so keep them private, short-lived and out of Git/artifacts unless encrypted with restricted access.

## Validation

Confirm a no-change normal plan after reconciliation. Test locking with two sandbox operations: a second writer should wait/fail, not overwrite concurrently. Do not force-unlock a running operation. Record the module output contract and one replacement example without applying it. Prove the backend bucket survives workload destroy and old state versions remain recoverable.

## Troubleshooting

| Failure | Evidence | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backend AccessDenied, provider reads work | Separate role/region/key and `.tflock` permissions | Repair backend scope |
| Lock held | Lock owner, operation ID, active CI run | Wait or cancel cleanly; force-unlock only proven orphan |
| Massive replacement after refactor | Addresses and moved blocks | Preserve identities before applying |
| Plan exit 1 reported as drift | Error diagnostics | Treat as failure, not exit 2 |

`prevent_destroy` is a configuration guard, not backup or an IAM deny. Removing a resource block removes that guard. `ignore_changes` can hide relevant drift; use it only for fields deliberately owned elsewhere. Avoid routine `-target`: partial graphs are an incident tool, not a deployment architecture.

## Cleanup

Remove local plan files and any `.terraform` cache when finished. Destroy workload resources before retiring the backend. Keep the state backend/version history until the exercise's retention window is complete; only its owner should remove versions and locks after verifying no active consumers. Never delete state as a substitute for destroying cloud resources.

## Interview preparation

**Why separate backend bootstrap?** The workload cannot depend on a backend that must already exist to initialize. Independent lifecycle and access boundaries avoid destroying the recovery record with the workload.

**How would you adopt a console-created resource?** Describe ownership, add matching configuration, use an import block, inspect a full plan for unexpected changes and commit the declaration. Import is an ownership mapping, not automatic design discovery.

**Why not automatically apply drift detection?** It may undo an intentional emergency action or adopt an attacker change. Detect, classify and review before choosing restore versus code update.

## Verify your understanding

Explain the difference between refresh-only and normal plans, capture exit codes correctly and show why a saved plan is sensitive. Completion requires a reviewed plan or clearly labelled static walkthrough, not a claim of deployment.

## Arabic takeaway

الـ state سجل ملكية وربط الموارد وممكن يحتوي أسرار. حطه في backend محمي مع versioning وlocking. اكتشاف drift مش قرار إصلاح تلقائي؛ افهم التغيير وراجع plan قبل أي apply.

## Sources

- [Terraform plan modes](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan)
- [Refactoring with moved blocks](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/modules/develop/refactoring)

## Learning objectives

Write OIDC audience/subject conditions, distinguish an unprivileged PR job from a privileged environment job and defend the integrity of a reviewed Terraform plan. Explain why an identity-token permission alone is not deployment authorization.

## Prerequisites

Use a new lab repository, not this repository's active deployment workflows. A sandbox administrator must create/import the GitHub OIDC provider and role. Choose a read/plan-only role initially; provider reads and backend writes for locking need distinct scoped permissions. A later apply role needs resource-specific creation/deletion and constrained PassRole permissions. Never use account-wide AdministratorAccess as the sample's default.

## The problem

A long-lived access key in repository secrets can be exfiltrated and reused elsewhere. GitHub OIDC exchanges a short-lived job identity for an STS session. The AWS role trust must verify the token audience and a narrow subject. A branch subject differs from an environment subject; if a job uses environment `cloud-lab`, trust that environment subject and protect its branches/reviewers in GitHub. Environment names alone do not enforce human approval.

An authenticated pipeline can still execute malicious Terraform. Providers, modules and external data programs are executable code. Do not run an untrusted fork PR with a deploy role, a writable state backend, or `pull_request_target` checkout of attacker code. Keep ordinary PR formatting/tests credential-free; run privileged plan only on reviewed refs, then require approval for apply.

## In this repository

`golang/content/labs/pipelines/aws-plan.yml.example` is an inert example copied manually into a separate sandbox repo. It is outside `.github/workflows/` here, so adding this course cannot trigger a cloud deploy. The current application build/GitOps workflows stay unchanged.

## Lab

Write the trust condition using your own account and a separate repository. This is a policy fragment for a role whose federated principal is the account's GitHub provider:

```json
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": {"Federated": "arn:aws:iam::ACCOUNT_ID:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"},
  "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
  "Condition": {
    "StringEquals": {
      "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",
      "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:OWNER/SANDBOX_REPO:environment:cloud-lab"
    }
  }
}
```

Replace all placeholders. Configure the GitHub environment's allowed deployment branch and required reviewers before granting the role. If your GitHub plan cannot enforce the intended reviewer feature, use a manual controlled alternative and record the limitation rather than claim protection exists.

Copy and read the example, pin action references to audited commit SHAs before using it for privileged jobs, then set repository variables for the sandbox region/state bucket and environment role ARN. The job requests `id-token: write` and `contents: read`, calls `configure-aws-credentials`, prints only `get-caller-identity`, initializes the backend and produces a plan. No `apply` step is included.

Validation exercise: run the plan job in the permitted environment, then intentionally change the role trust's subject to a different sandbox environment. Re-run and confirm federation is denied before Terraform can access AWS. Restore the exact condition. Do not display the OIDC token or STS credentials in logs. Capture only job identity, STS ARN and sanitized error code.

Design an apply workflow on paper: it must bind the approved commit, Terraform/provider lockfiles, state key, exact saved plan checksum, approval decision and apply identity. A second fresh plan is not the reviewed saved plan. Prefer short-lived restricted plan artifacts or regenerate/review close to deployment if secure artifact handling is unavailable.

## Validation

Pass criteria: no AWS access keys in GitHub secrets; exact `aud` and `sub` matching; disallowed environment fails; allowed job shows the expected assumed role; PR checks cannot assume it; no cloud apply step executes. A plan-only job still needs network access and read permissions and may expose data through plan output, so do not publish sensitive logs.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Check | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cannot get OIDC token | Job permissions and context | Enable id-token only for intended job |
| STS rejects token | Provider URL/audience/subject and environment use | Match exact claims; don't wildcard the organization |
| STS works, Terraform fails | Service permissions, backend, PassRole constraints | Separate trust success from resource authorization |
| Approval bypass | Actual environment protections and branch rules | Configure protections outside YAML |

Use job-level concurrency keyed by environment/state to reduce conflicting writers, while retaining backend locks as the authoritative state protection. Keep cloud sessions short and use meaningful session names for audit correlation.

## Cleanup

Disable/remove the lab workflow in the sandbox repo. Remove role policies and the lab role once no job uses it. Delete an OIDC provider only if you created it solely for this lab and have verified no other roles reference it. Preserve the real repository's federation and workflows.

## Interview preparation

**Why is `repo:ORG/*` too broad?** A compromised unrelated repository can gain the same identity route. Scope the exact repository and protected environment/ref, then constrain role permissions and session lifetime.

**Can fork PRs run Terraform safely?** Credential-free fmt/validate with controlled dependencies is different from a privileged plan. Never grant unreviewed code deployment credentials just because the event is called a PR.

**How do you audit a deployment?** Correlate commit SHA, approved plan digest, environment decision, workflow run and CloudTrail STS session. A green build without provenance does not answer who changed what.

## Verify your understanding

Explain branch versus environment subjects and demonstrate a deliberate trust failure in the sandbox. Present a sequence diagram from GitHub job token to STS session to backend/resource authorization. Label the example as plan-only.

## Arabic takeaway

الـ OIDC بيلغي المفاتيح الثابتة لكنه محتاج trust ضيقة ومراجعة للكود. افصل PR checks عن jobs اللي معاها صلاحيات، واحمِ environment فعلًا. نجاح STS مش معناه إن permissions أو الموافقة على النشر صح.

## Sources

- [GitHub OIDC in AWS](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/security-harden-deployments/oidc-in-aws)
- [AWS GitHub federation role](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_create_for-idp_oidc.html)
- [Configure AWS credentials action](https://github.com/aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials)
