text:
## Learning objectives

Build an end-to-end application platform rather than a set of isolated services. Prove request routing, workload identity, shared uploads and data durability, rehearse a target failure and explain the availability, security and cost decisions in a senior interview.

## Prerequisites

Finish AWS 01–06. Use AWS CLI v2, Terraform 1.10+, jq, SSM Session Manager plugin and a dedicated account with a reviewed deployment role. Obtain an **issued ACM certificate in the ALB region** and a DNS name you control. Supply a reviewed WordPress release version and SHA-256 of its official release archive. A certificate ARN or hash copied from an unrelated region/release will not work. The caller needs EC2/VPC/ELB/ASG/RDS/EFS/IAM/SSM/CloudWatch permissions; role creation and PassRole should be constrained to this lab's prefix.

This is paid infrastructure: two NAT Gateways/EIPs, ALB, EC2/EBS, Multi-AZ RDS, EFS, Secrets Manager and monitoring. Set a budget alert, price the chosen region, request any needed quotas and choose a same-day destroy deadline. Nothing in this repository applies it automatically. If budget is unavailable, do the static design/plan path and explicitly report that runtime acceptance was not performed.

## The problem

A single VM with local uploads loses availability when the machine fails and can lose data when replaced. This design sends HTTPS to an ALB spanning two AZs, forwards only from the ALB SG to private app instances, shares WordPress files on encrypted EFS, and connects to a private encrypted Multi-AZ RDS MySQL instance. The ASG maintains at least two instances. There is no public SSH or public DB. Instance management uses SSM, with egress through per-AZ NAT in this learning implementation.

```text
Client → DNS → ALB HTTPS (public A/B)
                  ↓ app SG allows ALB only
             ASG EC2 (private A/B) → EFS TLS shared files
                  ↓ DB SG allows app only
             RDS MySQL Multi-AZ (isolated A/B)
EC2 role → STS credentials → one RDS-managed secret
Private A/B → same-AZ NAT → IGW (bootstrap / SSM / AWS APIs)
```

ALB TLS ends at the listener; the private ALB→Apache hop uses HTTP in this lab. RDS connections enforce TLS in WordPress and EFS mounts use TLS. End-to-end ALB target TLS, WAF, CDN, image baking, EFS backups and central log shipping are explicit production hardening tasks, not implemented claims. The shallow health check deliberately avoids replacing every instance on a shared DB failure.

## In this repository

All deployable lab files are under `golang/content/labs/aws-wordpress/`; start with its README. Download individual files from `../labs/aws-wordpress/README.md`, or use your feature-branch checkout. The `modules/network` module owns the VPC/subnets/NATs. Root `main.tf` owns app, data and identity; `user-data.sh.tftpl` boots the instances. Examples are not imported by the live repository Terraform or GitOps manifests.

## Lab

1. In the lab directory, initialize without a backend and validate. Read every resource and the network module. Copy `terraform.tfvars.example` to a private ignored `.tfvars` file; replace region, certificate ARN, hostname, WordPress version/hash and your unique lab name. Keep passwords out of it: RDS manages the master password. For a real application, bootstrap a dedicated limited DB user and avoid continued master use.

```bash
cd golang/content/labs/aws-wordpress
aws sts get-caller-identity --query '{Account:Account,Arn:Arn}'
terraform init -backend=false
terraform fmt -check -recursive
terraform validate
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars
# Edit and review terraform.tfvars locally before the next command.
terraform plan -out=lab.tfplan
terraform show -no-color lab.tfplan
```

2. Verify two AZs, two NATs, app/database private addressing, SG references, IMDSv2 and encrypted storage. Review the AWS 05 backend setup if using shared state. Inspect cost and account one last time. **The following command creates paid resources; run only after your own explicit budget decision.**

```bash
terraform apply lab.tfplan
terraform output
```

3. Create a CNAME from the chosen lab hostname to the `alb_dns_name` output (use an alias if managing the hosted zone appropriately). Wait for DNS. The ALB rejects HTTP by redirecting to HTTPS; the certificate must match the hostname. Bootstrap validates the downloaded WordPress archive hash before unpacking and serializes shared EFS initialization across instances. Allow several minutes for packages, EFS mount and PHP setup; inspect cloud-init through SSM if targets stay unhealthy.

4. Finish WordPress's web installer promptly from your browser using a unique administrator password and disposable content. Add a post and an upload. Check each target's local readiness through SSM. Access through the public name, not the ALB hostname, to validate certificate/name behavior.

```bash
curl -I "https://$(terraform output -raw site_hostname)/"
curl -fsS "https://$(terraform output -raw site_hostname)/healthz.php"
curl -fsS "https://$(terraform output -raw site_hostname)/readyz.php"
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn "$(terraform output -raw target_group_arn)" --query 'TargetHealthDescriptions[].{ID:Target.Id,Health:TargetHealth.State}'
```

5. Run AWS 03's single-target failure drill while recording HTTPS results. Verify the post and uploaded image remain available after replacement. EFS and RDS protect against this instance-loss event, but you have not yet proved AZ failover or historical restore. Design the separate restore drill from AWS 04 and record RPO/RTO assumptions honestly.

## Validation

Acceptance evidence: `terraform validate`; reviewed resource plan; issued regional certificate; HTTPS without `-k`; two healthy targets in separate AZs; no public app IPs/SSH/DB; EFS mount with TLS; readiness proves a DB query; app IAM role can retrieve exactly its DB secret; post/upload survive one replacement; CloudWatch alarm exists; destroy inventory shows no residual chargeable lab resources.

Demonstrate a denied flow (direct external DB access), an allowed flow (ALB to app to DB) and identify which route/SG/IAM rule authorizes each boundary. Keep sanitized screenshots and a short architecture decision record. Never commit state, plan, logs with secrets or generated configuration.

## Troubleshooting

| Incident | First evidence | Recovery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TLS name error | ACM region/status and DNS hostname | Fix certificate/name; do not disable verification |
| Targets never register healthy | ASG activity, cloud-init, EFS DNS/2049, archive hash | Correct bootstrap input/dependency, refresh deliberately |
| DB 500 after secret rotation | Local generated DB config versus current secret version | Re-run secret-config refresh on instances; a production rotation hook is required |
| Posts visible, media missing | Shared EFS mount and file paths/permissions | Restore shared mount, not sticky-session masking |
| Terraform destroy fails | Dependency and RDS/secret finalization states | Wait for managed deletions; inspect exact failure before retry |

The RDS-managed credential is retrieved at boot; this example does not implement automatic in-place credential reload. For long-running use, implement and rehearse a rotation hook or connection strategy. This capstone intentionally uses a master account for initial WordPress setup; document the privilege reduction to a dedicated schema user before treating it as production.

## Cleanup

Remove the lab DNS record. Stop test traffic and SSM sessions. Inspect the destroy plan, then explicitly run it in the same lab directory and backend:

```bash
terraform plan -destroy -out=destroy.tfplan
terraform show -no-color destroy.tfplan
terraform apply destroy.tfplan
terraform state list
rm -f lab.tfplan destroy.tfplan
```

This ephemeral lab sets RDS deletion protection off and skips a final snapshot; it is destructive. Preserve any needed evidence/data first. Confirm no ASG/EC2, ALB, NAT, EIP, RDS, EFS/mount target remains for the lab prefix. Check managed secret deletion and manually created snapshots/backups separately. The separately bootstrapped state bucket is deliberately retained. Removing local state or stopping EC2 alone does not stop the bill.

## Interview preparation

**Why EFS and not local EBS for uploads?** Instance-local disks do not supply a shared multi-writer filesystem across independent ASG instances. EFS provides shared access but adds a dependency, permissions and backup requirements. An object-storage upload design is an alternative with different application integration.

**Is this architecture production-ready?** It demonstrates two-AZ compute/data boundaries, role-based secrets and TLS ingress. It still needs dedicated DB users, credential refresh, tested restore, hardened immutable images, centralized logs, patching, release controls and measured capacity/SLOs. State limitations directly.

**How would you explain this in five minutes?** Start from availability and data-loss requirements, draw the packet/identity/state paths, explain two tradeoffs (NAT cost and EFS sharing), show a timed incident and recovery, then outline DR and cost evidence.

## Verify your understanding

Present a five-minute design review and a ten-minute incident walkthrough. Keep a clear distinction between executed observations and planned extensions. Mark complete after runtime evidence, or label your evidence as static-only and schedule the paid validation separately.

## Arabic takeaway

المشروع النهائي خدمة WordPress كاملة: ALB بشهادة TLS، سيرفرات خاصة في AZs مختلفة، EFS للملفات وRDS للداتا. اثبت إن الخدمة والداتا فضلت موجودة بعد استبدال instance، وبعدها امسح كل موارد اللاب وراجع الفاتورة.

## Sources

- [AWS WordPress reference architecture](https://github.com/aws-samples/aws-refarch-wordpress)
- [RDS-managed master passwords](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/rds-secrets-manager.html)
- [EFS mount helper and TLS](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/efs/latest/ug/efs-mount-helper.html)
- [AWS Well-Architected](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html)

text:
## Learning objectives

Map tenant, subscription, Resource Group and resource scopes. Explain Entra identities versus Azure RBAC, select the right management/data roles and prove your active subscription before making a change.

## Prerequisites

Azure CLI and an approved sandbox subscription are required for the live lab. Obtain the subscription ID from its owner; do not choose the first subscription shown. Your account needs Resource Group creation permissions. Role assignments require additional authorization such as Role Based Access Control Administrator at the intended scope; Contributor alone does not grant that ability.

## The problem

An Entra tenant is the identity directory; a subscription is a resource/billing boundary associated with a directory. A Resource Group is a management/lifecycle scope within a subscription, not a network boundary. A VM in one RG can communicate with a VM in another if networking permits. Policies can deny resource configurations even when RBAC allows the caller's action.

Entra directory roles manage directory objects; Azure RBAC roles authorize Azure resources. Azure RBAC evaluates assignments at scopes with inheritance, applicable conditions and deny assignments. Resource management and service data planes are separate: being Contributor on a Storage Account does not automatically authorize blob reads via Entra. Some management roles can retrieve account keys, so distinguish nominal data roles from indirect access paths.

For comparison with AWS, an Azure subscription is not a perfect synonym for an AWS account. An Entra tenant can serve many subscriptions; managed identities and federated workload identities are service identities, not human user accounts. Build a scope diagram before memorizing role names.

## In this repository

Azure lab resources live under `golang/content/labs/azure-app/`. They never touch the Kubernetes cluster or learning application's user store. The capstone creates an isolated RG and uses an explicit subscription variable. Existing OIDC sign-in for this website remains unchanged.

## Lab

```bash
az login
export LAB_SUBSCRIPTION_ID='REPLACE_WITH_YOUR_SANDBOX_SUBSCRIPTION'
az account set --subscription "$LAB_SUBSCRIPTION_ID"
az account show --query '{subscription:id,tenant:tenantId,name:name,user:user.name}' -o json
export LAB_RG="cloud-learning-$(date +%s)"
export LAB_LOCATION=westeurope
az group create --name "$LAB_RG" --location "$LAB_LOCATION" --tags Purpose=cloud-learning
SCOPE=$(az group show --name "$LAB_RG" --query id -o tsv)
az role assignment list --scope "$SCOPE" --include-inherited --all --query '[].{Role:roleDefinitionName,Scope:scope,Type:principalType}' -o table
az role definition list --name Contributor --query '[0].permissions' -o json
az role definition list --name 'Storage Blob Data Reader' --query '[0].permissions' -o json
```

Compare `actions` to `dataActions`. List the exact effective assignment that permits RG creation and identify where it was inherited. On an organization-managed account, inability to list assignments can itself require a separate permission; do not interpret an empty/denied listing as proof of no access.

Create a local table with three principals (human operator, CI identity, VM managed identity) and three tasks (create VM, read blob, read Key Vault secret). Assign the narrowest appropriate scope and role for each. Have an authorized administrator optionally grant Reader to a disposable principal at this RG; demonstrate that it can inspect metadata but cannot create resources. Record the assignment ID if you do this extension so cleanup is precise.

## Validation

The account output must match the approved subscription and tenant. The new RG should have the Purpose tag. Your role matrix must distinguish management reads from blob/secret data reads, and describe which identity can grant roles. No VM or chargeable compute is created in this module.

## Troubleshooting

| Error | Evidence | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subscription not found | Active tenant and available subscriptions | Select correct directory; request access |
| AuthorizationFailed | Caller object ID, action and scope | Find missing role at the correct scope |
| RequestDisallowedByPolicy | Policy assignment/details | Use an approved region/SKU; don't broaden RBAC |
| Role granted, access still fails | Token refresh, propagation, correct principal object ID | Retry after propagation; verify scope and data plane |

Do not solve a data-plane failure by granting Owner. For service principals, application/client ID and service-principal object ID are different identifiers. Role assignments typically target the principal object ID.

## Cleanup

Delete only optional role assignments created for this lab using their recorded assignment IDs. Then remove this empty lab RG:

```bash
az group delete --name "$LAB_RG" --yes
az group exists --name "$LAB_RG"
```

Expect `false` after deletion finishes. Never delete an RG whose inventory includes resources owned by another exercise or team.

## Interview preparation

**Why can Contributor create a storage account but fail to read blobs?** Management actions and dataActions are distinct. Check the chosen auth mode, data role, scope and network boundary; keys can introduce alternate access if permitted.

**Where should CI permissions be assigned?** At the smallest resource/RG scope needed, with a separate controlled identity for bootstrap role assignments. Subscription-wide Owner is not a default deployment requirement.

**How do you prevent deployment to the wrong subscription?** Explicit account selection, provider subscription ID, pipeline identity checks, scoped service connections and policy. Naming conventions alone do not enforce the boundary.

## Verify your understanding

Draw your tenant/subscription/RG/resource hierarchy and explain inherited roles aloud. Keep a redacted account check, role matrix and cleanup result as evidence.

## Arabic takeaway

الـ Entra tenant للهوية، والـ subscription للموارد والفوترة، والـ Resource Group لإدارة دورة الحياة. فرّق بين إدارة المورد وقراءة الداتا داخله، واتأكد من subscription والـ scope قبل أي تعديل.

text:
## Learning objectives

Build a VNet/subnet boundary, inspect NSG rules and route-table associations, and explain private endpoint DNS resolution. Translate AWS mental models without assuming identical defaults or features.

## Prerequisites

Use the sandbox subscription from Azure 01. Azure CLI and dig/getent are useful. This basic lab creates networking control objects only; private endpoints, VMs, NAT and Network Watcher diagnostics may add charges. Runtime private-endpoint evidence is collected in Azure 07, which includes a private VM probe rather than testing only from your laptop.

## The problem

A VNet is the address/routing boundary. Azure provides system routes, which can be overridden by user-defined routes where applicable; longest prefix and route-source precedence matter. An NSG is stateful and can be associated with a subnet and/or NIC. When both apply, traffic must pass both. Lower priority numbers are evaluated first, and default rules still exist. Azure NSGs are not AWS stateless NACLs.

A private endpoint assigns a private IP in your VNet to a service's private connection. It does not automatically disable the service's public access or grant data authorization. Service endpoints instead extend service identity/connectivity from a subnet to the service's public endpoint; they are not interchangeable with private IP endpoints.

For Blob Storage, clients continue using `ACCOUNT.blob.core.windows.net`. Correct DNS resolves through the private-link name to a private A record from a linked private DNS zone. From on-premises, linking a zone to a VNet alone does not configure corporate DNS forwarding; Azure DNS Private Resolver or an appropriate forwarding design is needed. Testing only from a public laptop will not prove private DNS works for a VM.

## In this repository

The Azure capstone contains a VNet, app and private-endpoint subnets, a `privatelink.blob.core.windows.net` zone, a VNet link and a private-endpoint DNS zone group. Its storage account disables public network access. Its VM has no public IP and uses managed identity for blob access.

## Lab

Select your sandbox subscription and create a fresh RG. Preserve these names in the same shell:

```bash
az account set --subscription "$LAB_SUBSCRIPTION_ID"
export NET_RG="cloud-net-$(date +%s)"
az group create -n "$NET_RG" -l westeurope --tags Purpose=cloud-learning
az network vnet create -g "$NET_RG" -n lab-vnet --address-prefixes 10.60.0.0/16 --subnet-name app --subnet-prefixes 10.60.10.0/24
az network nsg create -g "$NET_RG" -n app-nsg
az network vnet subnet update -g "$NET_RG" --vnet-name lab-vnet -n app --network-security-group app-nsg
az network route-table create -g "$NET_RG" -n lab-routes
az network vnet subnet update -g "$NET_RG" --vnet-name lab-vnet -n app --route-table lab-routes
az network nsg rule list -g "$NET_RG" --nsg-name app-nsg --include-default -o table
az network vnet subnet show -g "$NET_RG" --vnet-name lab-vnet -n app --query '{prefix:addressPrefix,nsg:networkSecurityGroup.id,routeTable:routeTable.id}'
```

An empty user route table does not mean no routes: system routes still apply. Do not assume new private VMs receive implicit internet egress. Explicit outbound connectivity should be designed and is provided through a NAT Gateway in the capstone.

Optional deployed capstone drill: use VM Run Command from Azure 07 to run `getent ahostsv4 "$LAB_STORAGE_FQDN"` **inside the VM**, then inspect the blob private endpoint connection status and DNS A record. Controlled failure: remove only the capstone's VNet DNS link in a temporary Terraform change, review/apply it in the sandbox and repeat. Observe whether the name now resolves publicly and storage blocks the connection. Restore the link through Terraform and wait for DNS cache expiry. Record the exact result rather than assuming every resolver has the same cache.

## Validation

The app subnet must reference the intended NSG and route table. Distinguish configured UDRs from effective NIC routes, which can be inspected only once a NIC/VM exists. For the private endpoint drill, resolve the normal storage hostname to its expected private IP from the VM, confirm private endpoint Approved, and separately test data authorization.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | First check | Next layer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blob hostname resolves publicly in VM | Zone name, A record, VNet link, custom resolver | Endpoint connection and public-access policy |
| NSG appears to allow, connection times out | Both NIC/subnet effective NSGs and destination listener | Effective route and appliance return path |
| On-premises fails, Azure VM works | DNS forwarding and VPN/ExpressRoute path | Private endpoint routing and source controls |
| Private DNS succeeds, HTTP 403 | Managed identity role and firewall evidence | Network reachability is not data authorization |

Use `az network nic show-effective-route-table` and `az network nic list-effective-nsg` with the capstone NIC. For packet evidence, a paid Network Watcher connection troubleshoot/IP flow verify exercise can complement OS-level tests; static topology alone does not prove a listener is healthy.

## Cleanup

```bash
az group delete -n "$NET_RG" --yes
az group exists -n "$NET_RG"
```

Restore any controlled DNS change before the capstone's own cleanup. Delete the capstone via Terraform, not this temporary RG command. Check private endpoint NICs and links belong to the resource group you intend to remove.

## Interview preparation

**Private endpoint resolves to a public IP. Is RBAC the first fix?** No. Test resolution from the workload, zone/link/forwarding and endpoint state. RBAC is a separate layer after connectivity.

**NSG versus AWS NACL?** NSGs are stateful and attach to subnet/NIC scopes; AWS NACLs are stateless subnet controls. Do not carry over ephemeral return-rule assumptions mechanically.

**Can public access remain enabled with a private endpoint?** Yes. Disable/restrict it explicitly if required, then prove that intended clients use the private path and unwanted public access fails.

## Verify your understanding

Draw normal hostname → DNS chain → private IP → service → identity authorization. Show a deliberate DNS failure/recovery or label it as a planned runtime drill. Explain where effective routes differ from the table you configured.

## Arabic takeaway

الـ NSG stateful ومش نسخة من NACL. الـ private endpoint محتاج DNS صح من داخل الشبكة، ومش بيلغي public access أو بيدي صلاحيات للداتا لوحده. افصل DNS عن routing وعن RBAC في التشخيص.

## Sources

- [NSG evaluation](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/network-security-groups-overview)
- [Azure routing](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/virtual-networks-udr-overview)
- [Private endpoint DNS](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/private-link/private-endpoint-dns)
- [Explicit outbound connectivity](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-network/ip-services/default-outbound-access)

text:
## Learning objectives

Choose between Azure Load Balancer and Application Gateway, inspect a VM's application and agent health, and design a controlled VM Scale Set rollout across supported availability zones.

## Prerequisites

Use Azure CLI and review the Azure 07 capstone first. Live compute costs money and depends on regional SKU/quota availability. This module includes a local configuration design path plus commands for an already-deployed learner-owned VM. It does not create a second compute stack just to demonstrate a command.

## The problem

Azure Load Balancer is a layer-4 TCP/UDP service; Application Gateway is layer 7 for HTTP routing, TLS termination and optional WAF. An internal Standard Load Balancer can keep a service private. A public Application Gateway has a different cost, routing, subnet, certificate and health-probe model. Neither is a universal replacement for the other.

VM Scale Sets manage a group of VM instances; orchestration mode, image version, upgrade policy, health signals and zone support affect operational behavior. A running instance is not proof of a listening application. Health probes must reach the actual listener, and application health for repairs/rolling upgrades must be deliberately configured. An autoscale rule needs measured demand and realistic limits; a CPU threshold cannot repair a slow shared datastore.

Availability sets separate fault/update domains, while availability zones are distinct physical locations in supported regions. Zone redundancy requires service/SKU support, sufficient capacity and an application that tolerates partial loss. A single regional VM remains a single point of failure even if its disks are replicated.

## In this repository

The Azure capstone intentionally uses one private Linux VM and an internal Standard Load Balancer for a bounded troubleshooting exercise. It is **not** an HA/VMSS implementation. You will design and validate the VMSS/Application Gateway alternative here rather than claim that the smaller capstone already implements it. The AWS capstone supplies the concrete two-AZ autoscaling exercise.

## Lab

First write an ingress decision record with two rows: private TCP service through Standard Load Balancer and public HTTP hostname routing through Application Gateway. For each, record TLS location, source-IP behavior, probe source, subnet requirements, logs, cost and failure domain.

For a learner-deployed Azure 07 stack, export its exact identifiers and inspect VM status:

```bash
cd golang/content/labs/azure-app
RG=$(terraform output -raw resource_group_name)
VM=$(terraform output -raw vm_name)
NIC=$(terraform output -raw nic_name)
az vm get-instance-view -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --query 'instanceView.statuses' -o table
az network nic show -g "$RG" -n "$NIC" --query '{private:ipConfigurations[0].privateIPAddress,public:ipConfigurations[0].publicIPAddress}'
az network nic list-effective-nsg -g "$RG" -n "$NIC" -o json
az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --command-id RunShellScript --scripts 'systemctl is-active cloud-lab-app; curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz' --query 'value[].message' -o tsv
```

No public IP should be assigned. VM Run Command requires the VM agent and working platform connectivity, and executes with elevated privileges; it is not the same path as a client request through the load balancer.

Controlled failure: stop the lab service via Run Command, observe local curl failure and load-balancer backend health metrics, then restart it. Use Azure 07's probe VM test to prove the internal VIP is unavailable/recovered. VM power state should remain running throughout: this demonstrates the difference between machine health and application health.

Design extension: create a Terraform proposal replacing the single NIC/VM with a VMSS spanning supported zones, an image version, load-balancer backend association, health/repair configuration and bounded rolling upgrades. Review it with `terraform validate` and a sandbox plan after checking the provider schema; do not blindly apply because a sample SKU exists in a different region. For an Application Gateway variant, reserve its dedicated subnet and define a backend health path returning 200 without login redirects.

### VMSS hands-on extension

An inert, deployable configuration is provided as [vmss.tf.example](../labs/azure-app/vmss.tf.example). In the sandbox capstone directory, copy it to `vmss.tf`, check region/SKU zone support, then run `terraform validate` and a reviewed `terraform plan`. It adds two zonal instances to the internal LB pool and grants their managed identity Blob Data Reader. This is additional paid capacity; apply only in a separately budgeted window. The original single VM remains for comparison.

```bash
cp vmss.tf.example vmss.tf
terraform validate
terraform plan -out=vmss.tfplan
# Explicit extra-cost decision before terraform apply vmss.tfplan.
az vmss list-instances -g "$RG" -n lab-vmss --query '[].{ID:instanceId,Zone:zones,State:provisioningState}' -o table
az vmss get-instance-view -g "$RG" -n lab-vmss --instance-id 0
```

After a reviewed image/custom-data update is applied to the VMSS model, use `az vmss update-instances -g "$RG" -n lab-vmss --instance-ids 0` to update one lab instance, verify probe/client results, then update the next instance. This deliberately manual rollout teaches model versus instance state. It is not an automatic rolling-upgrade policy. Record observed capacity and stop if healthy capacity drops below the chosen threshold. Pin the image version for repeatability.

### Application Gateway hands-on extension

[application-gateway.tf.example](../labs/azure-app/application-gateway.tf.example) adds a dedicated subnet and a **private HTTP** L7 listener pointing at the internal LB. It is an intentionally visible extra hop for comparing L4/L7 health contracts, not the recommended minimal production path. The required v2 platform public IP has no public listener. In private tfvars set `app_client_cidrs = ["10.60.10.0/24", "10.60.30.0/24"]`, copy the example to `application-gateway.tf`, validate and review the added gateway cost before applying.

```bash
az network application-gateway show-backend-health -g "$RG" -n lab-http-gateway -o json
az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n lab-probe --command-id RunShellScript --scripts 'curl -fsS http://10.60.30.10/healthz' --query 'value[].message' -o tsv
```

With the optional probe VM enabled, deliberately change only the gateway probe path to a nonexistent path in Terraform, review/apply, observe backend health and client failure, then restore `/healthz`. Add HTTPS/certificate and WAF policy as a separate design exercise; this private HTTP extension does not claim TLS/WAF protection. For cleanup, leave activated files present while reviewing/applying the capstone's full destroy, then remove them. Deleting the files first without reviewing the resulting plan can obscure the intended lifecycle.

## Validation

Evidence includes VM running state, service stopped/running state, no public NIC IP, private probe results and recovery time. Your decision record must explain why this capstone cannot demonstrate multi-instance failover. The VMSS design must state min/max capacity and rollout failure policy rather than only a desired count.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Evidence | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| VM running, listener unavailable | systemd status and local curl | Restore process/configuration |
| Local curl works, LB fails | Backend association, probe path/port, NSG AzureLoadBalancer rule | Restore backend/probe reachability |
| Application Gateway 502 | Backend health reason, Host/TLS settings, listener | Fix contract between gateway and backend |
| Scale-out fails | Quota, SKU/zone availability and activity log | Choose approved capacity or request quota |

Do not open public SSH to debug an internal LB. Run Command/Bastion/private access are different management options with distinct cost and policy implications. An internal VIP cannot be tested directly from an unrelated public laptop.

## Cleanup

Restart the lab app if you stopped it. Remove temporary load generators and VMSS proposal files if not retained as review evidence. Destroy the underlying capstone with its own Terraform state. Any extra scale set/gateway you independently deployed needs its own inventory and destroy plan.

## Interview preparation

**Load Balancer or Application Gateway?** Start from protocol and routing requirements. L4 private TCP distribution fits Load Balancer; host/path routing, HTTP TLS policy and WAF can justify Application Gateway. Explain cost and observability tradeoffs.

**How do you prove an autoscaling setup is useful?** Drive bounded load, measure latency/error/queue depth and resource saturation, observe scale-out timing and verify the datastore can handle added concurrency. Instance count alone is not success.

**How do you roll back a bad VM image?** Keep a known-good immutable version, stop/abort the rollout, restore the desired version and refresh with healthy capacity. Handle schema compatibility separately.

## Verify your understanding

Explain running versus ready with your controlled outage. Present the VMSS extension as a design until tested, and name two ways a bad probe can trigger unnecessary repairs or hide real application failure.

## Arabic takeaway

الـ VM شغالة مش معناها التطبيق جاهز. اختار Load Balancer للـ L4 وApplication Gateway لاحتياجات HTTP وTLS/WAF. الـ VMSS محتاج health وrollout وخطة capacity؛ اللاب الصغير هنا مش HA لوحده.

## Sources

- [Load balancing options](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/technology-choices/load-balancing-overview)
- [VM Scale Sets](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/virtual-machine-scale-sets/overview)
- [Application Gateway backend health](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/application-gateway/application-gateway-backend-health)

text:
## Learning objectives

Use a VM managed identity without stored credentials, separate Blob/Key Vault data roles from management access, and explain metric, log and activity-log evidence. Design secret retrieval and rotation without embedding secret values in Terraform.

## Prerequisites

The practical runtime lab uses the Azure 07 VM and Storage Account. Azure CLI is required on your laptop; inside the VM the included Python app uses the metadata endpoint and standard library. Key Vault is a separately budgeted extension and is not silently created. Creating role assignments requires an appropriately privileged bootstrap identity.

## The problem

A system-assigned managed identity belongs to the lifecycle of its Azure resource; a user-assigned identity has an independent lifecycle and can be attached to multiple resources. Managed identity supplies an Entra token for a requested audience. It does not automatically grant authorization, network reachability or access to a secret.

Storage Blob Data Reader is a data-plane role. Key Vault Secrets User permits reading secret contents under the RBAC model; Key Vault Reader is metadata-oriented and is not equivalent. Choose one vault permission model deliberately and keep RBAC distinct from firewall/private endpoint rules. A 403 can reflect authorization or network restrictions; inspect the actual service error and the request's identity and route.

Azure Monitor is a family of facilities. Platform metrics, Activity Log (control-plane actions), resource diagnostic logs, VM guest logs and application telemetry are different data streams. A VM's stdout is not automatically in Log Analytics. Diagnostic settings, data collection rules/agents, retention and queries must be configured and costed deliberately.

## In this repository

The capstone disables shared keys and public Storage network access. It assigns the VM identity Storage Blob Data Reader on the account. The app's `/storage-check` requests an IMDS token for the Storage audience and lists the lab container; it never returns the token. No secret values or access keys are provisioned into Terraform state. The example's in-memory greeting is not a database-backed HA application.

## Lab

After deploying Azure 07 yourself, inspect identity and exact role assignment:

```bash
cd golang/content/labs/azure-app
RG=$(terraform output -raw resource_group_name)
VM=$(terraform output -raw vm_name)
SA=$(terraform output -raw storage_account_name)
PRINCIPAL=$(az vm show -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --query identity.principalId -o tsv)
STORAGE_SCOPE=$(az storage account show -g "$RG" -n "$SA" --query id -o tsv)
az role assignment list --assignee "$PRINCIPAL" --scope "$STORAGE_SCOPE" --query '[].{role:roleDefinitionName,scope:scope}' -o table
az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --command-id RunShellScript --scripts 'curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/storage-check' --query 'value[].message' -o tsv
```

Expected response: a small JSON result with a successful storage HTTP status, without a bearer token or blob body. Allow for role propagation. The storage container is created through the provider's management path, so the learner's public laptop does not need direct private blob access for provisioning.

Use the platform metric API to examine available VM metrics and a recent Activity Log window:

```bash
VM_ID=$(az vm show -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --query id -o tsv)
az monitor metrics list-definitions --resource "$VM_ID" --query '[].name.value' -o tsv
az monitor metrics list --resource "$VM_ID" --metric 'Percentage CPU' --interval PT1M --aggregation Average
az monitor activity-log list --resource-group "$RG" --offset 1h --query '[].{time:eventTimestamp,status:status.value,operation:operationName.value}' -o table
```

Key Vault extension: have an authorized lab operator create an RBAC-enabled vault with an approved network policy, create a disposable non-production secret, grant the VM identity Key Vault Secrets User at an intended scope and access it from the VM using a token for `https://vault.azure.net`. Validate only the version ID/HTTP status in shared evidence. Rotate the secret, verify retrieval of the new version and explain app caching/reload behavior. Record vault, role assignment and private endpoint/DNS IDs for cleanup. This extension requires its own commands/configuration review against current tenant policy; no production vault is used.

### Optional private Key Vault lab

A complete inert [key-vault.tf.example](../labs/azure-app/key-vault.tf.example) creates an RBAC vault with public networking disabled, a private endpoint/DNS link and a VM data-role assignment. It does not put a secret value in Terraform. Copy it to `key-vault.tf`, set a globally unique `vault_name` in private tfvars, validate and review the added cost before any apply. Follow tenant soft-delete/purge policies.

For this disposable exercise only, set `vault_data_role = "Key Vault Secrets Officer"`, review the scoped temporary permission and apply it in your sandbox. Download [vault-check.py](../labs/azure-app/vault-check.py) and copy it to the private VM through Run Command's script transport (no token/secret in arguments):

```bash
VAULT=$(terraform output -raw vault_name)
# Azure CLI loads the local script as the Run Command script body.
# Wrapper combines a local Python file into a shell script; values are lab identifiers only.
{ printf "python3 - %s --seed <<'PYTHON'\n" "$VAULT"; cat vault-check.py; printf '\nPYTHON\n'; } > /tmp/cloud-vault-seed.sh
az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --command-id RunShellScript --scripts @/tmp/cloud-vault-seed.sh --query 'value[].message' -o tsv
```

The script requests the Vault audience from IMDS and writes only a fixed harmless test string, then prints its version ID without a value/token. Change `vault_data_role` back to **Key Vault Secrets User**, review/apply, wait for verified role propagation, and run a read-only wrapper by omitting `--seed`. Read should succeed and `--seed` should eventually be denied under the read role. Role/managed-identity caches can take longer than a few minutes; capture observations without claiming immediate revocation. Never use a real secret as an argument or in this script.

To rehearse rotation, temporarily re-enable the explicitly scoped seed role, write a new disposable version, restore the read role and verify the version ID changes. Remove wrapper files afterward. Keep activated `.tf` files present during the capstone's full destroy so private endpoints, DNS and role ownership remain clear; only remove them after reviewed cleanup. Soft-deleted/purge-protected vaults follow tenant retention policy.

## Validation

Show the principal object ID/role scope with identifiers redacted. `/storage-check` should succeed from the VM and public anonymous blob access should fail. Prove a missing data role yields a different incident from a missing DNS link. Keep one metric query and one Activity Log event, explaining which logs are **not** collected by this lab.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | First evidence | Correction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No IMDS token | Identity attachment, audience, metadata header, no proxy | Fix token acquisition; don't store a fallback account key |
| Storage 403 with correct DNS | Role assignment/principal and propagation | Grant narrow data role or wait after verified assignment |
| Key Vault metadata visible, secret denied | Exact data role and permission model | Use Secrets User where appropriate |
| Log query empty | Diagnostic setting/agent, workspace, time range | Configure ingestion; absence is not proof of no incident |

Use a service error code and timestamps rather than only a screenshot saying 'Forbidden'. Avoid logging HTTP Authorization headers or dumping metadata token responses.

## Cleanup

Delete any optional Key Vault role assignment and disposable vault following the organization's soft-delete/purge-protection policy. Soft-deleted vaults may reserve names; purge protection cannot simply be bypassed for convenience. The capstone's identity and role are Terraform-owned and removed by its destroy. Keep diagnostic retention/cost settings in the cleanup inventory.

## Interview preparation

**Managed identity versus a stored service-principal secret?** Managed identity avoids distributing/rotating a client secret for supported Azure resources. It still needs authorization, correct token audience and working network paths.

**Why Contributor and Key Vault Secrets User separately?** One concerns management operations and one data access under RBAC. Broad management rights can still alter access boundaries, so separation of duties and restricted role-assignment permissions matter.

**What evidence do you need during a storage incident?** Request/error code, principal, role/scope, token audience, DNS/private endpoint state and recent control-plane changes. CPU charts alone cannot identify authorization failures.

## Verify your understanding

Draw the managed-identity token request and subsequent Storage request. Explain the difference between a token, a role assignment and a private endpoint. Show one successful private data access and one intentionally failed boundary test.

## Arabic takeaway

text:
## Learning objectives

Configure AzureRM with an explicit subscription, use Entra/OIDC for Blob state, explain lease locking and compare a backend authorization failure with a provider management failure.

## Prerequisites

Terraform 1.10+, Azure CLI and a dedicated subscription are required for live plans. Bootstrap a separate state RG/Storage Account/container with your administrator. The workload must not own its own backend lifecycle. The backend needs Storage Blob Data Contributor on the state container/account and working storage network connectivity; Azure resource Contributor alone is insufficient for Entra data access.

## The problem

Terraform's AzureRM provider manages Azure resources. The AzureRM backend reads/writes state blobs and leases them for locking. They are separate clients with separate authentication and network requirements. A private backend can be secure yet unreachable from a GitHub-hosted runner. Solve runner placement/private connectivity rather than temporarily opening all storage networks every deployment.

Use explicit Entra authentication, not an account key committed to `backend.tf`. The state blob may contain sensitive resource attributes, so enforce scoped data roles, encryption, versioning/soft-delete retention and restricted artifacts. A Blob lease prevents concurrent state writers; CI concurrency helps but does not replace the lease. `force-unlock` requires proof that the recorded operation is no longer active.

## In this repository

`labs/azure-app/versions.tf` pins a compatible provider major range and sets `subscription_id` explicitly. `backend.azurerm.tf.example` is inactive by default, keeping validation separate from backend use. The application Storage Account is private and ephemeral; it is **not** the state account. Existing production Terraform remains untouched.

## Lab

Start credential-free schema validation and provider inspection:

```bash
cd golang/content/labs/azure-app
terraform init -backend=false
terraform fmt -check
terraform validate
terraform providers
```

Have an authorized operator bootstrap the independent backend, enable blob versioning and soft delete, and assign your state identity the required data role. Select an allowed runner network. Copy the example and supply only non-secret identifiers:

```bash
cp backend.azurerm.tf.example backend.tf
terraform init -migrate-state \
  -backend-config="storage_account_name=$LAB_STATE_ACCOUNT" \
  -backend-config="container_name=tfstate" \
  -backend-config="key=cloud-learning/azure-app.tfstate"
```

The example uses `use_azuread_auth = true`. For local Azure CLI authentication ensure the logged-in tenant/subscription are correct. For CI use `use_oidc = true` and the documented workload identity environment variables, rather than setting a client secret. If your backend resolves through a private endpoint, validate DNS and 443 connectivity from the actual runner before blaming the token.

After a learner-deployed Azure 07 stack, change a harmless RG tag through the console. Run `terraform plan -refresh-only -detailed-exitcode` and distinguish 0 (no change), 2 (successful difference) and 1 (failure). Compare with a normal plan. Decide whether to restore the declared tag or intentionally update configuration, then verify a no-change normal plan.

Module-design exercise: separate VNet/private DNS into a reusable module with outputs for app subnet and endpoint subnet IDs. Keep state backend bootstrap and role-assignment administration outside that module. Use `moved` blocks for a refactor, inspect resource addresses and ensure the plan does not replace the VM/NIC merely because an address changed. The capstone remains a readable root module for first-time Azure diagnosis; this refactor is an assessed extension.

## Validation

Confirm state is stored under the intended unique key and a lease is held during an operation. Verify blob versioning/retention on the **backend** account. Show a plan using the correct provider subscription and evidence that the workload RG does not contain its state account. For static-only learners, label backend/lease checks as unexecuted.

## Troubleshooting

| Failure | Evidence | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backend 403, provider works | Data role and auth mode on state blob | Grant correct data role, not broader subscription Owner |
| Provider subscription error | Explicit subscription/tenant and identity scope | Fix provider settings separately |
| Backend timeout | Runner DNS, storage firewall/private path | Restore connectivity |
| Lease held after CI crash | Lease/lock ID and active operation inventory | Unlock only confirmed orphan; preserve state version |

Do not run two independent states against the same resources. Moving state between backends requires a reviewed migration and secure backup, not copying only the Terraform source. `terraform init -reconfigure` ignores a previous backend configuration; it is not equivalent to migrating existing state.

## Cleanup

Remove temporary plans and working caches. Destroy the workload before retiring the backend. Keep the independent backend's retained versions until the recovery policy permits deletion, then have its owner remove the dedicated state resources. Never delete a live state blob just to clear a lock.

## Interview preparation

**Why does Azure Contributor still get backend 403?** Blob state uses a data plane, and Entra data authorization requires the appropriate role at its scope. Also check network policy and identity before granting anything.

**How do self-hosted runners help private state?** They can reach private DNS/endpoints from an approved VNet. That solves a network requirement, while identity, runner isolation and state permissions still need separate controls.

**How do you handle an orphaned lease?** Verify the owner/run has ended, record the lock metadata, preserve a state recovery point and use the documented unlock flow. Never break an active writer's lock to speed up a deployment.

## Verify your understanding

Draw provider API traffic and backend Blob traffic as separate lines with separate roles. Explain the difference between migrate-state and reconfigure, and demonstrate a harmless drift review without automatically applying it.

## Arabic takeaway

الـ provider والـ backend اتنين clients مختلفين؛ نجاح واحد مش دليل إن التاني شغال. الـ state على Blob محتاج data role وlease locking ومسار شبكة صحيح، ويفضل يكون عمره مستقل عن موارد التطبيق.

## Sources

- [AzureRM backend](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/backend/azurerm)
- [Terraform Azure authentication](https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hashicorp/azurerm/latest/docs/guides/azure_cli)
- [Terraform state on Azure Storage](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/developer/terraform/store-state-in-azure-storage)

text:
## Learning objectives

Explain Entra federated credentials, bind audience/issuer/subject to a specific pipeline context and design comparable review controls in GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps Pipelines.

## Prerequisites

Use a separate sandbox repository/Azure DevOps project. An authorized operator must create an Entra application/service principal or a supported user-assigned managed identity, the federated credential and scoped Azure RBAC. Do not create client secrets. Azure DevOps service-connection configuration and protected checks require project permissions beyond editing YAML.

## The problem

Federation replaces a reusable client secret with a short-lived identity assertion from the CI platform. It does not grant Azure access by itself: the target service principal/identity needs scoped RBAC. GitHub's issuer/subject are not Azure DevOps's issuer/subject. Copy the values issued for the actual service connection rather than adapting a GitHub trust string by guesswork.

A GitHub environment can bind a job to a subject such as `repo:OWNER/REPO:environment:azure-lab`; branch/reviewer restrictions must exist in the environment's settings. Azure DevOps workload-identity service connections have their own trust configuration, pipeline authorization and approvals/checks. Avoid 'grant access to all pipelines' unless that broad boundary is intentionally justified.

## In this repository

Read `labs/pipelines/azure-github-plan.yml.example` and `azure-pipelines.yml.example`. They are inert plan-only examples, outside the active CI directories. They use a separate state backend and do not add an apply path to the production repository. The examples use readable action versions; pin audited immutable references before privileged real use.

## Lab

GitHub path: create a sandbox environment `azure-lab`, restrict its branch and reviewers, and create the matching Entra federated credential with issuer `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`, audience `api://AzureADTokenExchange` and the exact environment subject. Assign the identity only the sandbox resource roles and backend Blob data role it needs. Put non-secret client/tenant/subscription IDs in environment variables/vars; they are identifiers, not a substitute for credential validation.

Copy the GitHub example to the sandbox repository, set its Terraform directory and state identifiers, and run it through manual dispatch after reviewing the commit. The job requests an OIDC token, performs `azure/login`, sets the Terraform OIDC variables, checks the active account and runs plan only. A local Azure CLI login is not an explanation for why a CI job can authenticate.

Azure DevOps path: create an Azure Resource Manager service connection using **workload identity federation**, scope it to the sandbox, and authorize only the intended pipeline. Use the actual issuer/subject Azure DevOps provides when configuring the federated identity. Attach approvals/checks on the service connection/environment outside YAML. Copy the example to a sandbox project and ensure Terraform is installed on its pinned runner image or trusted setup task before invoking it.

Controlled failure: change only the sandbox federated subject to a nonmatching environment/service-connection subject, re-run and capture the failed token exchange without exposing the assertion. Restore the trust and rerun. Then test a successful token exchange with an insufficient data role on a *dedicated* backend test scope to distinguish identity from state authorization. Do not remove shared organizational assignments.

## Validation

Both examples should stop after a reviewed plan, use no static client secret, report the expected sandbox subscription and reject an unintended job context. Record identity, subject, role scope, backend key, commit SHA and approval boundary. No actual resource apply is necessary to prove federation or backend access.

## Troubleshooting

| Error | Investigate | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No matching federated identity | Exact issuer/audience/subject | Use values for this CI system/context |
| Login succeeds, resource denied | RBAC scope and role propagation | Correct narrow assignment |
| Backend fails only on hosted runner | Private network/DNS reachability | Use approved runner network |
| Pipeline edits bypass approval | External checks and service-connection authorization | Enforce checks outside attacker-editable YAML |

A reviewed plan can become stale if state changes. Revalidate expected state/commit and use bounded artifact retention. A plan file may contain secrets; avoid unrestricted artifact downloads and public logs. Serialize jobs per environment/state key and retain backend locking.

## Cleanup

Disable sandbox workflows/pipelines and remove their dedicated service connections/federated credentials. Remove role assignments only for those lab principals. Delete the dedicated app/identity only after verifying no other jobs use it. Keep the production repository's current CI and cloud identity untouched.

## Interview preparation

**GitHub OIDC versus Azure DevOps federation?** Same objective—short-lived workload identity—but different token issuer/subject setup and authorization controls. Exact trust claims and scoped RBAC matter more than the platform name.

**Why put approvals outside YAML?** A contributor who can modify a pipeline should not be able to remove the only deployment gate in the same change. Resource/environment checks create an independently administered boundary.

**How do you divide plan and apply?** Credential-free checks for untrusted code; privileged plan for reviewed refs; approval bound to commit/plan/state; narrowly privileged apply and audit trail. Never equate a successful login with deployment approval.

## Verify your understanding

Explain a failed exchange and a failed backend authorization as different incidents. Present a pipeline diagram for each CI system, including the controls configured outside YAML and the absence of static secrets.

## Arabic takeaway

GitHub وAzure DevOps يقدروا يستخدموا federation من غير client secret، لكن issuer وsubject مختلفين. احمِ service connection والـ environment من برّه YAML، وافصل plan عن apply والموافقة الفعلية.

## Sources

- [Azure login with GitHub OIDC](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/developer/github/connect-from-azure-openid-connect)
- [Azure DevOps workload identity service connections](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/library/connect-to-azure?view=azure-devops)
- [Azure DevOps approvals and checks](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/process/approvals?view=azure-devops)

text:
## Learning objectives

Deploy a private application path with explicit outbound connectivity, prove private endpoint DNS and data authorization from inside the VNet, and distinguish load-balancer, service, DNS and identity incidents. Produce an interview-ready incident report with rollback and cleanup evidence.

## Prerequisites

Use a sandbox subscription, Azure CLI and Terraform 1.10+. Supply a local SSH **public** key for VM creation, though the lab uses Run Command and never opens SSH. Check quotas and availability for the selected VM size/region. Price VM/disks, NAT/public IP, Standard Load Balancer, Storage and private endpoint charges; set a destroy deadline. Budget alerts are not hard spending limits.

No application secrets or account keys are needed. Your deployment identity needs resource management rights for the lab RG and permission to assign the Storage Blob Data Reader role; separate bootstrap role assignment from routine CI where appropriate. Use local state initially or the independent backend from Azure 05.

## The problem

The application is a small Python HTTP service with `/healthz` and `/storage-check`. It runs on a VM with no public IP behind an **internal** Standard Load Balancer. The VM obtains a Storage token through managed identity and lists a private Blob container via a private endpoint and linked DNS zone. The Storage Account disables shared keys, public access and anonymous containers. A NAT Gateway supplies explicit outbound access for bootstrap, agent and Azure APIs; it does not provide inbound access.

```text
Management: Azure CLI → VM Run Command (platform agent)
Client test: temporary private probe VM → internal LB :8080 → app VM :8080
App VM → normal Blob hostname → private DNS → Blob private endpoint
App VM → IMDS managed identity token → Storage data role → list container
App VM/probe subnet → NAT → internet egress (not inbound SSH)
```

This is a secure-boundary troubleshooting lab, not a highly available production implementation. It has one application VM, no public website, and internal HTTP rather than TLS. Azure 03's extension designs VMSS/zones/Application Gateway. A real deployment needs TLS, resilient compute, diagnostic ingestion, backups where state is added, hardened images and tested releases.

## In this repository

Use `golang/content/labs/azure-app/` only. `main.tf` creates the isolated RG, VNet/subnets/NSG, NAT, load balancer, private storage endpoint/DNS and VM managed identity/role. `app.py` uses Python's standard library, checks the metadata header and never logs tokens. `cloud-init.yaml.tftpl` installs the service without external package dependencies. A second probe VM is optional and disabled by default. Download the README at `../labs/azure-app/README.md` for file links.

## Lab

```bash
cd golang/content/labs/azure-app
az account set --subscription "$LAB_SUBSCRIPTION_ID"
az account show --query '{subscription:id,tenant:tenantId}'
terraform init -backend=false
terraform validate
cp terraform.tfvars.example terraform.tfvars
# Edit subscription_id, public key path, unique storage name, region and budgeted VM size.
terraform plan -out=azure-lab.tfplan
terraform show -no-color azure-lab.tfplan
```

Read the plan for private addressing, NSG scope, public Storage disabled, shared-key access disabled, private endpoint connection and role assignment. **Applying creates paid resources; proceed only after your own cost/account review.**

```bash
terraform apply azure-lab.tfplan
RG=$(terraform output -raw resource_group_name)
VM=$(terraform output -raw vm_name)
FQDN=$(terraform output -raw storage_fqdn)
az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$VM" --command-id RunShellScript --scripts "getent ahostsv4 $FQDN; systemctl is-active cloud-lab-app; curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/storage-check" --query 'value[].message' -o tsv
```

Wait for VM agent readiness and RBAC propagation; do not mask an ongoing failure as eventual consistency indefinitely. The normal Blob hostname must resolve to the endpoint's private IP from the VM. The app should return a successful Storage status without returning a token or blob payload.

To prove the actual client path, enable `enable_probe = true` in your private tfvars, review/apply the incremental cost, then use the probe VM (same VNet, no public IP) to call the **internal LB** output on port 8080 through Run Command. Calling the LB from the backend VM itself can involve hairpin behavior, so use the separate probe:

```bash
PROBE=$(terraform output -raw probe_vm_name)
VIP=$(terraform output -raw internal_lb_ip)
az vm run-command invoke -g "$RG" -n "$PROBE" --command-id RunShellScript --scripts "curl -fsS http://$VIP:8080/healthz; curl -fsS http://$VIP:8080/storage-check" --query 'value[].message' -o tsv
```

Controlled incidents, one at a time:

1. Stop `cloud-lab-app` via app VM Run Command. Confirm VM remains running, local curl fails and probe-to-LB fails after health detection. Restart it and measure recovery.
2. Temporarily remove the private DNS VNet link through a reviewed Terraform edit, repeat name lookup and storage-check from the VM, then restore. Record cache effects and endpoint error evidence.
3. In the sandbox only, remove the app's Storage data role through a reviewed config edit, keeping identity attached. Token acquisition should still work, but storage access fails after authorization caches/propagation. Restore the assignment and verify recovery. Don't print the token to prove acquisition; service error/status is sufficient.

## Validation

Keep five checks: no public app/probe NIC IP; private Blob DNS IP; public Storage access blocked; managed-identity data request succeeds; probe→internal VIP succeeds. Include one failed/recovered process, DNS and role boundary with timestamps. The Terraform role resource should target the VM principal and the lab account scope, not the subscription.

## Troubleshooting

| Failure | Evidence | Repair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Run Command unavailable | VM agent/platform connectivity, provisioning status | Restore explicit outbound/agent health |
| Local 8080 works, VIP fails | Probe VM path, LB backend NIC association, NSG probe rule | Correct LB/probe network contract |
| Storage-check timeout | DNS private IP, endpoint approval, NSG/route | Restore private connectivity |
| Storage-check 403 | Service code, exact principal/data role | Repair RBAC; allow propagation after verification |
| Deploy fails on storage container | Provider management-plane support/schema, subscription policy | Read provider error; do not expose account keys |

## Cleanup

Restore all intentional edits before destroying so ownership matches state. Review and apply a destroy plan in this same directory/backend:

```bash
terraform plan -destroy -out=azure-destroy.tfplan
terraform show -no-color azure-destroy.tfplan
terraform apply azure-destroy.tfplan
terraform state list
az group exists --name "$RG"
rm -f azure-lab.tfplan azure-destroy.tfplan
```

Expect an empty workload state and `false` for the deleted RG. Check the Activity Log for completion and inventory any resources you manually added outside the RG, especially diagnostic workspaces/backups. The independently bootstrapped state account remains. Deleting an RG manually first is not the ordinary Terraform lifecycle.

## Interview preparation

**App can get an identity token but cannot read Storage. What next?** Check requested audience, principal, data role/scope and propagation separately from DNS/private endpoint/firewall. A token proves authentication, not authorization or network reachability.

**How do you prove the load balancer works?** Test its VIP from a separate allowed client, inspect backend association/probe rules, and induce a controlled process failure. A localhost curl on the backend proves only the listener.

**What would you change for production?** Add resilient compute and rollout, TLS ingress, least-privilege data scope, observability, image patching, explicit SLOs, tested restore if persistent app data is introduced, and cost governance. Keep these as proposed improvements until implemented and measured.

## Verify your understanding

Deliver an incident report: symptom, hypothesis, evidence, isolated cause, minimal fix, verification and prevention. Compare Azure private endpoint/managed identity boundaries with AWS endpoint/instance-profile boundaries without claiming they are identical.

## Arabic takeaway

ابنِ مسار خاص كامل واختبره من جوه الشبكة ومن client منفصل. نجاح token مش نجاح Storage، ونجاح localhost مش نجاح الـ load balancer. اعزل عطل الخدمة عن DNS وعن RBAC، وارجع كل حاجة ثم امسح موارد اللاب.

- [Managed identity on an Azure VM](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/managed-identities-azure-resources/how-to-use-vm-token)
- [Private endpoints for Storage](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-private-endpoints)
